meta.blurb: Epictetus was born a slave, tradition says, yet he taught that no one can take your inner freedom. His Enchiridion is a short handbook on what you control, what you do not, and how to stay calm either way.
meta.bible: The Enchiridion: a short handbook of 53 brief chapters of practical advice, compiled by Arrian from the teaching of Epictetus; the Greek title means something held in the hand, a handbook. Epictetus: a Greek Stoic philosopher born about AD 50 in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey; tradition says he was born into slavery in Rome and was lame; he was freed, taught in Rome and later in Nicopolis in Greece, wrote nothing himself, and died about AD 135. Arrian: his student, who recorded his talks and gathered the Enchiridion. Stoicism: the school of philosophy that teaches that peace and goodness come from governing our own judgements and accepting what we cannot change. Socrates: the philosopher of Athens who died in 399 BC and whom Epictetus held up as a model. Chrysippus: a famous Stoic writer of the third century BC. Cleanthes: an earlier Stoic teacher whose prayer is quoted at the end. Euripides: the Greek poet quoted at the end. Anytus and Meletus: the men who accused Socrates. Zeus, the gods and Destiny: how Epictetus and the Stoics of his time spoke of the order of the world. Rome, Nicopolis, Greece: the places of his life. The Olympic Games: the athletic contest he uses as an image. Epaphroditus: Epictetus's master in Rome, a freed slave who worked as a secretary to the emperor Nero. Nero: the Roman emperor from AD 54 to 68. Musonius Rufus: a Roman Stoic teacher whose lectures Epictetus attended. Domitian: the Roman emperor who sent philosophers out of Rome, about AD 93. Hierapolis: Epictetus's birthplace, in what is now Turkey. Zeno of Citium: founder of Stoicism in Athens about 300 BC; the school took its name from the Stoa, the painted colonnade where he taught. Augustus: the first Roman emperor, founder of Nicopolis. Actium: the sea battle of 31 BC. Discourses: Arrian's notes of Epictetus's talks, in eight books of which four survive. Diogenes and Heraclitus: Greek philosophers Epictetus names as models. Euphrates: a famous speaker mentioned in chapter 29. Polynices and Eteocles: brothers who fought over the throne of Thebes. Pythian Apollo: the god of the oracle at Delphi. Marcus Aurelius: Roman emperor from AD 161 to 180, a Stoic who quoted Epictetus. Rusticus: Marcus Aurelius's teacher who lent him notes of the Discourses. Simplicius: a philosopher who wrote a long commentary on the Enchiridion about AD 530. James Stockdale: an American naval pilot, shot down in 1965 and held in North Vietnam for years, who credited Epictetus. Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck: modern therapists who said Stoic ideas influenced their methods. Plato: the writer whose dialogue Crito records the words of Socrates. Crito: a friend of Socrates. Nicopolis: the Greek city where Epictetus taught. Obol: a small Greek coin. Roman citizens, praetor, senator and consul: Roman offices and ranks mentioned in the book. Delphi: the place of the oracle of Pythian Apollo. Key idea: some things are up to us (our opinions, choices, wishes and actions) and some are not (our bodies, property, reputation and offices). Voice and tone: direct, practical, quietly humorous and firm; most beats name the chapter of the Enchiridion they retell; the first ten and the last ten also tell the life of Epictetus and what became of the book; everything is attributed to Epictetus; nothing is invented; respectful of every faith.

beats.scene: A baby is carried into a crowded house in a Greek hill town
beats.summary: Epictetus is born about AD 50 in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, and tradition says he was born into slavery.

beats.scene: A young servant waits behind a rich man's chair in Rome
beats.summary: He is taken to Rome and serves Epaphroditus, a freedman who worked for the emperor Nero, and tradition says he became lame.

beats.scene: Students sit on benches listening to a stern teacher in a Roman hall
beats.summary: After he is freed he studies with the Stoic Musonius Rufus and learns to teach philosophy.

beats.scene: Soldiers in red cloaks watch a line of teachers leaving Rome
beats.summary: The emperor Domitian sends philosophers out of Rome, about AD 93, and Epictetus moves to Nicopolis in Greece.

beats.scene: Young men from many lands gather in a plain schoolroom by the sea
beats.summary: In Nicopolis Epictetus opens a school and teaches by talking, questioning and giving blunt, kind advice.

beats.scene: A tall young man writes quickly on wax tablets while his teacher speaks
beats.summary: Epictetus wrote nothing himself, but his student Arrian took notes of his talks, which became the Discourses.

beats.scene: A young man folds a small scroll and ties it with string
beats.summary: Arrian also gathered the most useful sayings into a short handbook that he called the Enchiridion.

beats.scene: A hand grips a small scroll beside a short dagger on a table
beats.summary: Enchiridion is a Greek word for something held in the hand, and it was also used for a small dagger.

beats.scene: Marble pillars of the Painted Porch in Athens glow in the sun
beats.summary: Stoicism began in Athens about 300 BC with Zeno of Citium, who taught under a painted colonnade called the Stoa.

beats.scene: A reader sits calmly at a window as a storm blows outside
beats.summary: The book promises peace of mind, and its method begins with a single sharp question: what is up to you?

beats.scene: A man draws a chalk line on the ground between two heaps
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Epictetus divides everything in life into what is up to us and what is not.

beats.scene: Four glowing objects labelled by a thought bubble hang over a man's head
beats.summary: Chapter 1: what is up to us is our opinion, our impulse, our desire and our aversion; in short, our own doing.

beats.scene: A man looks at his house, his purse, a crowd and a mayor's chain
beats.summary: Chapter 1: what is not up to us is our body, our property, our reputation and our public offices.

beats.scene: A bird flies free from an open cage above a courtyard
beats.summary: Chapter 1: what is up to us is free by nature, and no one can block it or hold it back.

beats.scene: A man chases a coin that rolls down a hill while a thief watches
beats.summary: Chapter 1: what is not up to us is weak, can be taken away, and belongs in the end to other people.

beats.scene: A man shakes his fist at the sky while his lamp blows out
beats.summary: Chapter 1: if we treat what is not ours as ours, we are blocked and upset, and we blame gods and people.

beats.scene: A man walks through a quiet crowd with no one stopping him
beats.summary: Chapter 1: if we claim only what is truly ours, no one can force or hinder us, and we have no enemy.

beats.scene: A traveller sets down a heavy sack on a mountain path
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Epictetus warns that great goals need our whole effort, so some things must be put aside completely.

beats.scene: A man stops at a doorway to look hard at a shadowy shape
beats.summary: Chapter 1: when a harsh impression arrives, say to it: you are only an impression, not the thing itself.

beats.scene: A man holds a lamp up to a shadowy shape on a wall
beats.summary: Chapter 1: test every impression by asking whether it concerns what is up to us, and if not, say it is nothing to me.

beats.scene: A traveller reaches eagerly toward a distant golden fruit on a high branch
beats.summary: Chapter 2: desire promises to get what you want, so the person who fails to get it is unhappy.

beats.scene: A man leaps back from a snake coiled on a stone
beats.summary: Chapter 2: aversion promises to avoid what you fear, so the person who falls into it is unhappy.

beats.scene: A sick man lies in bed while a sunrise lights the window
beats.summary: Chapter 2: if you fear things like illness, death and poverty that are not up to you, you will be unhappy.

beats.scene: A man stands firm as a river of coins and rumours flows past
beats.summary: Chapter 2: turn aversion away from those things and aim it only at what is up to us and wrong.

beats.scene: A man puts down a heavy basket of wishes outside a gate
beats.summary: Chapter 2: for now take desire away altogether, since it fixes on things that are not up to us.

beats.scene: A man leans carefully over a table to choose one small stone
beats.summary: Chapter 2: use only the plain impulse to choose and to refuse, lightly, gently and with reservation.

beats.scene: A woman pours water from a clay jug and smiles at it
beats.summary: Chapter 3: whatever charms you or is useful or loved, remember its nature, starting with a jug.

beats.scene: A father kisses his small child on the forehead at dusk
beats.summary: Chapter 3: when you kiss your child, say that you kiss a human being, and you will not be wrecked if they die.

beats.scene: A crowded public bath where people splash, shove and shout
beats.summary: Chapter 4: before an action, picture what it will be, as at the public bath where people splash and push.

beats.scene: A man steps into the water calmly with his hands open
beats.summary: Chapter 4: say, I want to bathe and also to keep my will in harmony with nature, and do the same with every task.

beats.scene: A man stares at a dark door while a cat sits behind it
beats.summary: Chapter 5: people are upset not by things but by their opinions about things.

beats.scene: A thinking man sits beside a stone cup in a small dim cell
beats.summary: Chapter 5: if death were truly terrible, Socrates would have thought so, but he did not.

beats.scene: A man steps calmly through a door into a plain bright room
beats.summary: Chapter 5: the terror is the opinion that death is terrible, so the thing to fix is the opinion.

beats.scene: A man stops on a path and points at his own chest
beats.summary: Chapter 5: when we are blocked, upset or grieved, we should blame no one else but our own opinions.

beats.scene: Three men in a row: one points ahead, one at his chest, one smiles
beats.summary: Chapter 5: the untaught blame others, the beginner blames himself, and the trained person blames no one.

beats.scene: A man proudly leads a fine white horse down a village street
beats.summary: Chapter 6: do not be proud of what is not your own; if the horse said I am beautiful, that would be bearable.

beats.scene: A man looks inside himself as a lamp glows in his chest
beats.summary: Chapter 6: what is your own is your use of impressions, and being proud of that is being proud of a good of your own.

beats.scene: A passenger picks up shells on a shore while the ship waits
beats.summary: Chapter 7: life is like a voyage, and on shore you may gather a little shell or bulb, but listen for the captain.

beats.scene: A man holds a child's hand on the beach as the captain waves
beats.summary: Chapter 7: if wife and child are given in place of shell and bulb, nothing prevents it, but if the captain calls, run to the ship.

beats.scene: An old man sits on the sand near the ship's plank
beats.summary: Chapter 7: if you are old, do not go far from the ship, so that you are not missing when the captain calls.

beats.scene: A traveller smiles as rain falls on a muddy road
beats.summary: Chapter 8: do not ask for events to happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do, and life will go well.

beats.scene: A lame traveller walks slowly with a stick and a calm face
beats.summary: Chapter 9: illness hinders the body and lameness hinders the leg, but not the will unless the will allows it.

beats.scene: A man looks at a stone in the road and then steps around it
beats.summary: Chapter 9: say this on every occasion, and you will find that the hindrance is to something else, not to you.

beats.scene: A man stands calm and strong as wind and rain blow past him
beats.summary: Chapter 10: on every occasion turn to yourself and ask what power you have for dealing with it.

beats.scene: A man looks at a handsome stranger, a hill and an angry voice
beats.summary: Chapter 10: if you see a handsome person you will find self-control, in hard work endurance, in abuse patience.

beats.scene: A traveller hands a small key back to the innkeeper at dawn
beats.summary: Chapter 11: never say I have lost it; say I have given it back.

beats.scene: A parent kneels at an empty small bed with a quiet face
beats.summary: Chapter 11: if your child or your wife dies, say they have been given back, and the same for your land.

beats.scene: A man sees a stranger lead away his cart and nods slowly
beats.summary: Chapter 11: but he who took it is wicked, you say; why should you care through whom the giver asked for it back?

beats.scene: A traveller sweeps an inn room and places its keys on a hook
beats.summary: Chapter 11: while it is given, take care of it as travellers do of an inn, as something that is not your own.

beats.scene: A man carries a lamp up a stair into a bright room
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Epictetus returns again and again to the picture of life as something lent, which shapes the way we hold everything.

beats.scene: A worried man frowns over a ledger at his desk
beats.summary: Chapter 12: if you wish to make progress, give up thoughts like if I neglect my affairs, I will have nothing to live on.

beats.scene: A man sleeps peacefully on a hard bed beside an empty bowl
beats.summary: Chapter 12: it is better to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in plenty with a troubled mind.

beats.scene: A boy spills a jar of oil while a man stays calm
beats.summary: Chapter 12: begin with small things; if your oil is spilled, say it is the price of peace of mind.

beats.scene: A man hands coins to a market seller and receives a bundle
beats.summary: Chapter 12: nothing is got for nothing; peace of mind is bought with what we are willing to give up.

beats.scene: A man calls from a doorway and no one answers
beats.summary: Chapter 12: when you call a servant, he may not come or may not obey, but he is not so powerful that your peace depends on him.

beats.scene: A man in plain clothes stays quiet while others laugh at his clumsy answer
beats.summary: Chapter 13: if you want to improve, be content to be thought foolish about outside things.

beats.scene: A man sits down with his family at the end of a long day
beats.summary: Chapter 14: it is silly to wish that your children, wife and friends should live forever, since that is not up to you.

beats.scene: A man frowns at a spoiled dish and a tired cook
beats.summary: Chapter 14: it is equally silly to wish that others should never make a mistake, as if you wanted a fault not to be a fault.

beats.scene: A man walks along an open road with a light pack
beats.summary: Chapter 14: but if you wish not to fail in your own desires, you can do that, so practise on what you can do.

beats.scene: A wide-open gate stands in a wall with sunlight pouring through
beats.summary: Chapter 14: whoever wishes to be free must neither want nor avoid what depends on others, or he must be a slave.

beats.scene: A table of dishes passes slowly from hand to hand at a banquet
beats.summary: Chapter 15: behave in life as at a banquet; when a dish comes to you, take a polite share.

beats.scene: A guest lets a platter go by and watches it with a smile
beats.summary: Chapter 15: when a dish passes by, do not hold it back, and if it has not come yet, do not stretch out for it but wait.

beats.scene: A man holds a child, a purse and a chain of office lightly
beats.summary: Chapter 15: do this with children, a wife, office and wealth, and one day you will be fit to dine with the gods.

beats.scene: Two bearded old men sit calmly, one in a barrel, one writing
beats.summary: Chapter 15: if you take nothing and despise even what is set before you, you will be a partner of the gods, like Diogenes and Heraclitus.

beats.scene: A man sits beside a weeping friend and rests a hand on his shoulder
beats.summary: Chapter 16: when you see a friend weeping, remind yourself that it is his judgement about the event that hurts him.

beats.scene: A man speaks softly to a sad friend while his own face stays calm
beats.summary: Chapter 16: do not hesitate to comfort him with words, even to groan with him, but take care not to groan inside.

beats.scene: An actor in a rough beggar's costume stands on a bare stage
beats.summary: Chapter 17: you are an actor in a play whose author chooses the part, short or long, poor or royal.

beats.scene: An actor bows low as the lamps of the theatre glow
beats.summary: Chapter 17: your task is to act the part you are given well, and the choosing of it belongs to someone else.

beats.scene: A black raven croaks from a bare branch above a quiet road
beats.summary: Chapter 18: when a raven croaks as a bad omen, do not be carried away, but tell yourself it signifies nothing to you.

beats.scene: A man smiles at the raven and walks on in the sunlight
beats.summary: Chapter 18: any sign can be turned to your benefit, for whatever happens it is in your power to gain from it.

beats.scene: A calm athlete watches others compete in a distant arena
beats.summary: Chapter 19: you can be unbeatable if you enter no contest that you cannot win by your own effort.

beats.scene: A man in a plain cloak watches a splendid procession pass
beats.summary: Chapter 19: when you see someone honoured or powerful, do not hurry to call him happy.

beats.scene: A man with an open hand smiles at a rich man's parade
beats.summary: Chapter 19: if the real good is in our power, neither envy nor jealousy has any place.

beats.scene: A man lays down a purple robe and steps outside into the open air
beats.summary: Chapter 19: do not wish to be a consul or a senator but to be free, and the only way is to care little for outside things.

beats.scene: A man laughs calmly as a neighbour shouts at him across a fence
beats.summary: Chapter 20: remember that it is not the person who insults you who harms you but your opinion that you are insulted.

beats.scene: A man waits with eyes closed and counts slowly before he speaks
beats.summary: Chapter 20: when someone irritates you, win time and delay, and you will more easily master yourself.

beats.scene: A traveller with a small bag looks toward a far horizon at sunset
beats.summary: Chapter 21: keep death and exile before your eyes every day, so that nothing will seem mean.

beats.scene: A man smiles in an empty room with only a bed and a lamp
beats.summary: Chapter 21: if you do, you will never think anything is shabby and never desire anything too much.

beats.scene: Friends laugh at a man holding a book while he stays calm
beats.summary: Chapter 22: if you turn to philosophy, prepare to be laughed at by many who will say he has come back a philosopher.

beats.scene: A man stands steady at a post on a wall at dawn
beats.summary: Chapter 22: hold to what seems best to you as a post given by a god, and those who laughed may admire you later.

beats.scene: A man sets down a mask and looks in a mirror
beats.summary: Chapter 23: if you turn outward to please someone, you have lost your plan of life; be a philosopher to yourself.

beats.scene: A man sits alone in a plain room as dinner guests pass the window
beats.summary: Chapter 24: do not let thoughts afflict you such as, I will live without honour and be a nobody.

beats.scene: A man stands calm as a tall rich official walks by
beats.summary: Chapter 24: if lack of honour is an evil, no one else can put you in evil any more than in shame.

beats.scene: A man stands outside a crowded door while a feast goes on inside
beats.summary: Chapter 24: it is not your business to get a post or an invitation, so how is it a dishonour not to get them?

beats.scene: A friend holds out an empty purse while a man shakes his head
beats.summary: Chapter 24: your friends will have no money from you, and you cannot make them Roman citizens, so who said these were in our power?

beats.scene: A man holds a small scale with a heart on one side
beats.summary: Chapter 24: I will gladly help my friends if I can keep my honour and loyalty, but I will not lose them to give money.

beats.scene: A shoemaker holds out shoes while a smith holds up a sword
beats.summary: Chapter 24: your country needs no porticoes or baths from you; a smith does not make shoes, and a shoemaker does not make arms.

beats.scene: A man teaches a young person to be honest while others listen
beats.summary: Chapter 24: if you help to make one more faithful and modest citizen, you have done your country real good.

beats.scene: Two men at a market stall: one pays coins, the other walks away empty-handed
beats.summary: Chapter 25: if another is honoured above you, ask what price you paid for it; a lettuce costs a small coin.

beats.scene: A man at home in lamplight eats simple bread while a feast glows afar
beats.summary: Chapter 25: if you were not asked to the feast, you did not pay the host's price, and you still have your freedom.

beats.scene: A servant drops a cup that shatters while a calm man looks on
beats.summary: Chapter 26: when another person's cup breaks we say that it happens; we should react the same way when our own breaks.

beats.scene: A group of neighbours gather quietly around a grieving family
beats.summary: Chapter 26: when another man's child or wife dies, we all say that is human; we should remember this when our own dies.

beats.scene: A bowman shoots at a target set up on a sunny hillside
beats.summary: Chapter 27: as a target is not set up in order to be missed, no evil by nature exists in the world.

beats.scene: A man hands the keys of his house to a rude stranger
beats.summary: Chapter 28: we would be angry if someone handed our body to a stranger to push around.

beats.scene: A man shuts a door on a shouting visitor and stands in the quiet
beats.summary: Chapter 28: yet we hand our minds to anyone who insults us and feel no shame at being upset.

beats.scene: An athlete trains in the sun, sweating and covered in dust
beats.summary: Chapter 29: before you start anything, think what comes before and after it, as in training for the Olympic Games.

beats.scene: A runner eats plain food at a table while others feast
beats.summary: Chapter 29: an athlete must keep a diet, avoid delicacies, train at fixed hours in heat and cold, and obey the trainer.

beats.scene: Two wrestlers are tangled in dust in a ditch beside an arena
beats.summary: Chapter 29: in the contest you may be dug into the ditch, dislocate your arm, swallow dust and still lose.

beats.scene: Children play at wrestlers and trumpeters in a dusty yard
beats.summary: Chapter 29: people who try one thing after another, like children playing at games, are like apes imitating what they see.

beats.scene: A man looks at his own arms and legs and thinks hard
beats.summary: Chapter 29: before you try, look at your own nature, since different people are built for different things.

beats.scene: A man weighs a bag of coins against a plain wooden bowl
beats.summary: Chapter 29: philosophy costs, but it buys tranquillity, freedom and constancy; do you wish to pay?

beats.scene: A man stands alone, one hand reaching inward, one hand outward
beats.summary: Chapter 29: you must be one person, good or bad, working either on your inner self or on outside things.

beats.scene: A grown son helps his elderly father across a busy street
beats.summary: Chapter 30: duties are measured by relationships; a father is to be cared for and given way to.

beats.scene: A son sits quietly at a table while a stern father scolds
beats.summary: Chapter 30: but he is a bad father, you say; were you given a good father, or a father?

beats.scene: Two brothers face each other across a gate, one with arms crossed
beats.summary: Chapter 30: if a brother wrongs you, keep your own place toward him and ask what you must do to stay true to nature.

beats.scene: A magistrate, a neighbour and a soldier stand in a line
beats.summary: Chapter 30: in the same way look at the relations of neighbour, citizen and general and you will find your duties.

beats.scene: A man bows his head quietly before a simple stone altar
beats.summary: Chapter 31: the chief part of piety is to hold right opinions about the gods and to accept what happens.

beats.scene: A farmer, a sailor and a merchant look up at a dark sky
beats.summary: Chapter 31: people who lose wives, children or goods blame the gods because they put good and evil in outside things.

beats.scene: Two brothers in armour glare at each other before a throne
beats.summary: Chapter 31: Polynices and Eteocles became enemies because each thought the throne was a good, Epictetus says.

beats.scene: A man lays fruit and flowers on a plain altar at sunrise
beats.summary: Chapter 31: make offerings by the custom of your country, cleanly, not carelessly or meanly or beyond your means.

beats.scene: A man waits before a priest at a temple door
beats.summary: Chapter 32: when you go to a diviner, remember you do not know what will come, but you know what kind of thing it is.

beats.scene: A man listens to a prophet with open hands and no fear
beats.summary: Chapter 32: whatever he says, it is nothing to you, and you can use it well, and no one can stop you.

beats.scene: A man weighs a short question beside a long road
beats.summary: Chapter 32: Socrates held that we should ask a diviner only about outcomes that reason cannot work out.

beats.scene: A man runs toward a friend being attacked on a lonely road
beats.summary: Chapter 32: if a friend or your country is in danger, you do not ask whether to help, for reason already says so.

beats.scene: An angry priest points a man out of a temple gate
beats.summary: Chapter 32: Epictetus recalls that Apollo threw a man out of his temple for failing to help a friend who was killed.

beats.scene: A man stands alone and then among people with the same face
beats.summary: Chapter 33: set a certain character and pattern for yourself, and keep it both alone and with other people.

beats.scene: A man at a feast keeps his lips together as others talk loudly
beats.summary: Chapter 33: be silent for the most part, speak only when needed, and use few words.

beats.scene: Friends chatter by the arena wall while a quiet man listens
beats.summary: Chapter 33: do not talk about gladiators, horse races, food and drink, and above all do not talk about other people.

beats.scene: A man smiles quietly in a crowd that laughs loudly
beats.summary: Chapter 33: do not laugh much, or at many things, and avoid oaths if you can.

beats.scene: A clean man sits next to a dusty man on a bench
beats.summary: Chapter 33: if you spend time with a dirty person you will get dirty too, however clean you are.

beats.scene: A man stands in a plain room with a bed and a bowl
beats.summary: Chapter 33: take things for the body only as far as bare need, and cut away what is for show or luxury.

beats.scene: A man smiles gently while a gossiping neighbour points at him
beats.summary: Chapter 33: if you hear that someone has criticised you, answer that he does not know your other faults.

beats.scene: A man sits calmly in a stadium as the crowd leaps and shouts
beats.summary: Chapter 33: at the games, shout for no one and wish only that what happens should happen and that the winner should win.

beats.scene: A man listens politely at a poetry reading with folded hands
beats.summary: Chapter 33: do not go to people's readings rashly, but if you go, keep your gravity and calm.

beats.scene: A man stands before a grand door with a servant barring it
beats.summary: Chapter 33: before visiting a great man, say that he may be out, that the door may be shut, and go anyway.

beats.scene: A man at a dinner table speaks while others look bored
beats.summary: Chapter 33: do not often talk about your own deeds and dangers, for others do not enjoy hearing about your affairs.

beats.scene: A man in a circle of friends turns a joke into a quiet smile
beats.summary: Chapter 33: avoid provoking laughter and avoid obscene talk, and show by silence or a frown that you dislike it.

beats.scene: A man looks at a tempting cake on a table, then walks away smiling
beats.summary: Chapter 34: when a pleasure tempts you, let it wait, and picture how you will feel afterward.

beats.scene: A man weighs a feeling of pleasure against a feeling of pride
beats.summary: Chapter 34: set against the pleasure the satisfaction of having won, and choose by looking at both.

beats.scene: A man works openly in a busy square while people stare
beats.summary: Chapter 35: when you do what you know is right, do not hide it, even if most people think otherwise.

beats.scene: A man at a dinner party takes the largest piece of meat
beats.summary: Chapter 36: to choose the largest portion is of value for the body but worthless for keeping a social character.

beats.scene: A host smiles warmly as a guest takes a fair share
beats.summary: Chapter 36: when you dine with another, remember not only what the food is worth to your body but your respect for the host.

beats.scene: A man in a stranger's costume looks lost on a stage
beats.summary: Chapter 37: if you take on a role beyond your strength, you disgrace yourself in it and neglect the one you could have done.

beats.scene: A man walks carefully along a rocky path, watching his feet
beats.summary: Chapter 38: as you watch your steps to avoid a nail, take care not to harm the part of you that judges and chooses.

beats.scene: A man pauses at a fork in a road and thinks before he acts
beats.summary: Chapter 38: if we guard our judgement in each action, we will undertake everything more safely.

beats.scene: A shoemaker measures a foot beside a pile of fancy golden shoes
beats.summary: Chapter 39: the body is the measure of what we need to own, as the foot is the measure of the shoe.

beats.scene: A shelf of shoes grows from plain leather to gold and purple
beats.summary: Chapter 39: once we pass the measure there is no limit, as a shoe goes from plain to gilded, then purple, then embroidered.

beats.scene: A woman and a man stand quietly dressed in plain clothes
beats.summary: Chapter 40: Epictetus says people who put their hopes on looks should learn they are honoured for modesty and self-respect.

B1B2: Epictetus was born about AD 50 in Hierapolis, a town in what is now Turkey. Tradition says that he was born into slavery, and his Greek name simply means acquired.

As a young man he was taken to Rome and served Epaphroditus, a freed slave who worked for the emperor Nero. Tradition says he was lame, though stories differ about whether a cruel master or an illness caused it.

After he was freed, Epictetus studied with Musonius Rufus, a respected Roman Stoic who taught that philosophy must be lived and not just discussed. That training shaped almost everything he would teach in the years that followed.

Around AD 93 the emperor Domitian ordered philosophers to leave Rome, and Epictetus was among those who went. He settled in Nicopolis, a young city in northwestern Greece, and taught there for many years.

His school in Nicopolis was plain, and students came from many parts of the Roman world to sit in front of him. He taught by asking questions, joking and speaking bluntly, and he expected his students to change how they lived.
Epictetus wrote nothing himself, but one of his students, Arrian, took careful notes while he spoke. Those notes became the Discourses, a long work in eight books, of which four have survived.

Arrian also picked out the most useful sayings and arranged them in a short handbook, which he called the Enchiridion. It has only fifty-three brief chapters and is small enough to read in a single sitting.
In Greek, enchiridion means something held in the hand, and the word was also used for a small dagger. A handbook like this was meant to be kept close and used whenever trouble came.
Epictetus belonged to the Stoic school, which began in Athens about 300 BC with Zeno of Citium. Its teachers met under a painted colonnade called the Stoa, and that is how the school got its name.
The Enchiridion promises something simple: a calmer mind, whatever happens to you. To reach it, Epictetus asks us to start with one sharp question, which is what is truly up to you?
Epictetus opens his handbook by dividing everything in life into two kinds. Some things are up to us, he says, and some things are not.
What is up to us, he explains, is our opinion, our impulse, our desire and our aversion. In other words, it is all that is our own doing, including what we want and what we try to avoid.
What is not up to us includes our body, our property, our reputation and our public offices. In short, it is everything that is not our own doing.
Epictetus says that what is up to us is free by nature, and nobody can block it or hold it back. A person's own opinions and choices, in other words, cannot be locked away or taken by force.
What is not up to us is weak, he says, and it can be taken away at any moment. It really belongs to other people or to fortune, however much we may feel it is ours.
If we treat what belongs to others as if it were our own, we will be blocked and upset. We will end up blaming both gods and people for our troubles.
But if you claim as yours only what really is yours, no one will ever be able to force you or hinder you. You will have no enemy, because nobody will be able to do you any real harm.
Epictetus warns that such big goals need your whole effort, not a half-hearted try. Some things must be put aside completely, and others must wait for now.
He then gives a simple method for dealing with hard moments when they arrive. Whenever a harsh impression arrives, say to it, you are only an impression and not the thing you appear to be.
Next, test the impression by the rule you have, asking whether it concerns what is up to you. If it does not, be ready to say that it is nothing to you.
The second chapter of the handbook begins with a simple fact about desire. Desire promises that you will get what you want, so the person who fails to get it is unhappy.
Aversion, the wish to avoid something, works in the same way. It promises that you will escape what you dislike, so the person who falls into it is unhappy.
Epictetus names the things people fear most, such as illness, death and poverty. If you fear things that are not up to you, he says, you will always be unhappy.
So he tells us to turn our fear toward the wrong things that we ourselves might choose to do. That is where fear belongs, because only there can we really avoid what we dread.
For the time being, he says, we should remove desire altogether from things that are not up to us. If we want what we cannot control, we are bound to be let down sooner or later.

What remains is only the plain impulse to choose and to refuse, and Epictetus says to use it lightly and gently. We should also keep a reservation in mind, so that we are not shocked if our plans do not work out.
In the third chapter he asks us to remember what a thing really is, whether it charms us or is merely useful. If you like a clay jug, say that you like a jug, and you will not be upset if it breaks.
The same advice applies to the people whom you love most of all. When you kiss your child, say that you are kissing a human being, and you will not be crushed if the child dies.
The fourth chapter begins with a scene that everyone knew, a trip to the public baths. People there splash, push, shout and steal, so picture just what the place will be like before you go.

Then say to yourself that you want to bathe and also to keep your will in harmony with nature. In the same way, he says, do this before every action, and you will not be upset when something gets in the way.
The fifth chapter contains one of the most famous ideas in the whole book. People are disturbed not by things themselves but by the opinions they hold about those things.
Death, for example, is nothing terrible in itself, or it would have seemed terrible to Socrates. Socrates faced it calmly, which shows that the terror lies somewhere else.
The terror is in the opinion that death is terrible, says Epictetus. That is why the thing to work on is the opinion, not the world outside us.
So when we are blocked, upset or grieved, we should never blame someone else. Instead we should blame ourselves, which really means our own opinions about what has happened.

Epictetus describes three stages of progress, and the first two are easy to recognise in ourselves. Untaught people blame others for their troubles, beginners blame themselves, and a person who is fully trained blames neither.
In the sixth chapter he warns us not to be proud of what is not our own. If a horse boasted that it was beautiful, that would be bearable, but it is odd for its owner to boast of it.

So what is really our own, according to Epictetus, and what is it that we may rightly be proud of? It is our use of impressions, the way we handle our thoughts, and pride in that is pride in a true good.
The seventh chapter compares life to a voyage, and the comparison is a gentle one. When the ship stops, you may go ashore and pick up a shell or a bulb, but keep your mind on the ship.
If a wife or a child is given to you instead of a shell, nothing prevents you from having them. But if the captain calls, you must run to the ship and leave everything behind, without looking back.
An old man, Epictetus adds, should not go far from the ship at all. Otherwise the captain may call, and he will not be there to answer.
The eighth chapter gives a short rule that many readers find hard to accept. Do not ask for events to happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do, and life will go well.
In the ninth chapter Epictetus considers illness, which hinders the body, and lameness, which hinders the leg. Neither of them hinders the will, he says, unless the will itself agrees to be hindered.
Say this to yourself on every occasion that comes your way, he tells us. You will find that whatever has been hindered, it is something else and not you.
The tenth chapter gives a question to ask whenever something happens to you. Turn to yourself and ask what power you have for dealing with it.
If you see a handsome person, you will find self-control as your power against desire. If it is hard work, you will find endurance, and if it is abuse, you will find patience.
The eleventh chapter changes the way we talk about loss. Never say that you have lost something, says Epictetus, but say that you have given it back.
If your child dies, he says, the child has been given back. If your wife dies, she has been given back, and if your property is taken, that too has been returned.
But he who took it is a bad man, you may say. What does it matter to you through whom the giver asked for his gift back?
While the gift is yours, take care of it as travellers take care of an inn. A traveller does not weep on leaving his room, because he always knew that it was not his own.
Epictetus keeps coming back to the idea that everything we have is lent to us. If we remember this, we will hold our possessions and our loved ones more lightly and more gently.
The twelfth chapter is for those who want to make progress. Give up thoughts such as, if I neglect my affairs I will have no income.
It is better, he says, to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in plenty with a troubled mind. Peace of mind is worth more than comfort that comes with constant worry.

Begin your training with small things, Epictetus advises, because they cost so little to lose. If a little oil is spilled or a little wine is stolen, say that this is the price paid for peace of mind.
Nothing is got for nothing, he reminds us, and that is as true of peace as of anything else. A calm mind has to be bought, and the coin we pay with is the small things that we are willing to lose.
When you call a servant, he adds, remember that the servant may not hear you, or may hear and not obey. But he is not so powerful that your peace of mind depends on him.

The thirteenth chapter asks for something hard: if you want to improve, be content to be thought foolish about outside things. Do not try to seem wise, and if people think you are somebody important, learn to distrust yourself.

In the fourteenth chapter Epictetus says it is silly to wish that your children, wife and friends will live forever. You are wishing for things that are not up to you, and you are asking to own what belongs to others.
In the same way, it is silly to wish that other people should never make mistakes. You are asking for a fault not to be a fault, which no wish can bring about.
But if you wish not to fail in your own desires, you can do that. So practise on the things that really are within your power, and give your effort to them.
Epictetus ends the chapter with a rule about freedom. Whoever wishes to be free must neither want nor avoid what depends on others, or else he must become a slave to them.
The fifteenth chapter says that life should be treated like a banquet. When a dish is carried around to you, put out your hand and take a polite share.
If the dish passes you by, do not try to stop it. If it has not yet come to you, do not reach for it with your desire, but wait until it arrives.
Epictetus says to behave in the same way toward children, a wife, an office and wealth. If you do, you will one day be a worthy guest at the banquet of the gods.
He then goes even a step further than that. Whoever despises even what is set before him, he says, will share the gods' rule as well as their table, as Diogenes and Heraclitus did.

The sixteenth chapter is about a friend who is crying, perhaps because his son has gone abroad or his property is lost. Remind yourself that what hurts him is not the event, which does not hurt another person, but his own judgement about it.
Do not hesitate to comfort him with words, and even to groan with him if the moment calls for it. But take care that you do not groan inside as well.
The seventeenth chapter reminds you that you are an actor in a play. The author chooses the play, and it may be short or long, as he thinks best.

If the author wants you to play a poor man, a lame person, a ruler or a private citizen, play that part well. Your business is to act the given part skilfully, and the choosing of it belongs to someone else.
The eighteenth chapter deals with omens, which many people feared in those days. When a raven croaks, do not let the impression carry you away, but tell yourself that it signifies nothing for you.

The sign may concern your body, your property or your reputation, but it does not concern you. To you every omen is favourable if you wish it to be, because from whatever happens you can gain some benefit.
In the nineteenth chapter Epictetus says that you can be unbeatable. All you have to do is to enter no contest in which victory does not depend on you alone.
When you see someone honoured above others, or holding great power, or highly praised, do not be carried away by the impression. Do not be in a hurry to declare that such a person is truly happy.
If the essence of the good lies in what is up to us, he says, there is no place for envy or jealousy. We will not need what another person has, because our own good cannot be taken away by anyone.
You will not wish to be a praetor, a senator or a consul. You will wish to be free, and the only road to that is to care little for what is not up to you.
Epictetus says that it is not the person who abuses or strikes you who insults you. It is your own opinion that these things are insulting.

So when someone irritates you, remember that it is your own opinion that irritates you. Try not to be carried away by the impression, and win time by waiting, and you will master yourself more easily.
The twenty-first chapter asks us to keep death and exile before our eyes every day. Of all the things that appear terrible, he says, we should think chiefly of death.
If you do this, you will never think anything is shabby, and you will not desire anything too much. Remembering that we are mortal puts small worries into proportion and keeps our wishes in check.
The twenty-second chapter warns that if you turn to philosophy, you should prepare to be laughed at by many. They will say that he has come back a philosopher, and ask where he got such a proud look.

Do not put on a proud look, but hold to what seems best to you as a post given to you by a god. If you stand firm, those who laughed will later admire you, but if you give in, you will be laughed at twice.

The twenty-third chapter says that if you ever turn outward to please someone, you have lost your plan of life. Be content to be a philosopher in everything, and if you want to seem one, it is enough to seem so to yourself.
In the twenty-fourth chapter Epictetus lists thoughts that should not trouble you. One of them is the worry that you will live without honour and be a nobody anywhere.
If lack of honour were a real evil, he says, another person could no more cause it than cause your shame. Only your own choices can bring you to either of them.
Is it your business to get a post or to be invited to a dinner? Not at all, says Epictetus, so how can missing them be a dishonour?
But my friends will be left without help, you say, and what will become of them? What kind of help do you mean, when they will not get money from you and you cannot make them Roman citizens?
Who told you that these things are in our power, Epictetus asks the imagined friend. I will gladly help if I can keep my honour and loyalty, but I will not lose them to win you money.
And what of your country, you may say, which will go without your help? It will not get grand halls or baths from you, but a smith does not make shoes, and a shoemaker does not make weapons.
It is enough if each person does his own work well. If you help to make one more faithful and modest citizen, you have done your country real good.

The twenty-fifth chapter asks how to feel when someone is honoured before you at a dinner or a meeting. If these things are good, be glad that he got them, and if they are bad, do not grieve that you did not.

A lettuce costs a small coin, and if you do not pay it, you have lost nothing, because you still have the coin. In the same way, if you were not invited to the dinner, you did not pay the host's price of praise and attendance.

The twenty-sixth chapter finds a lesson in a broken cup, because nature's will can be learned from things on which we all agree. When another person's cup is broken, we say that these things happen, and we should be just as calm when our own cup breaks.
Then he asks us to carry the same attitude over to greater things. When another man's child dies, everyone says that this is the human lot, but when our own dies, we cry out in grief.
The twenty-seventh chapter is a single sentence about the world. As a target is not set up in order to be missed, so nothing that is evil by nature exists in the world.
In the twenty-eighth chapter he asks us to imagine a strange thing. If someone handed your body over to any stranger, you would be angry.

Yet you feel no shame in handing your own mind to anyone who insults you, so that it is disturbed and confused. Why should a stranger's rude word be allowed to disturb the part of you that decides and judges?

The twenty-ninth chapter says that before you begin anything you must think about what comes before it and after it. His example is the Olympic Games, a prize that he agrees is a fine one to wish for.
An athlete must keep to a strict diet, avoid rich foods and train at fixed hours in heat and cold. He must hand himself over to his trainer just as he would to a doctor.
Then in the contest he may be dug into a ditch, dislocate an arm or twist an ankle. He may swallow a lot of dust, be beaten and in the end still lose.

Epictetus says that people who start without thinking are like children who play at being wrestlers one day and trumpeters the next. They are like apes that copy whatever they see, and they never give their whole soul to any one thing.
So first look at the matter, and then look at your own nature to see whether you can bear it. Look at your arms, your thighs and your back, because different people are made for different things.

He then states plainly what the path will cost you, since you must work hard and be laughed at by those you meet. Consider whether you wish to pay that price for tranquillity, freedom and constancy, and if not, do not even begin.

Do not be like children who are a philosopher now, a tax collector later and then a public speaker. These things do not go together, since you must be one person, working either on your inner self or on outside things.
The thirtieth chapter says that duties are measured by relationships. If he is your father, you should care for him, give way to him and bear his harsh words.
But what if he is a bad father, someone may say, and treats me unfairly? Were you given a good father by nature, Epictetus replies, or only a father?
Epictetus gives another example, the brother who wrongs you. Keep your own place toward him, and ask not what he does but what you must do to stay true to nature.

Another person cannot harm you unless you let him, he says, because you are harmed only when you think you are. In the same way, you will find the duties of a neighbour, a citizen or a general by looking at the relationship each time.

The thirty-first chapter says that the chief part of piety toward the gods is to hold right opinions about them. We must believe that they exist and govern all things well and justly, and we must accept whatever happens.

People blame the gods when they think that things outside them are good or bad. The farmer, the sailor, the merchant and those who lose their wives and children all complain against the gods when things go badly.
Epictetus gives a famous example from the old Greek legends. Polynices and Eteocles, who fought over the throne of Thebes, became enemies because each of them thought the throne was a good.

Piety also has a practical side, he adds, and it follows the habits of the place where we live. We should make our offerings to the gods by the custom of our country, in a clean way, not carelessly, meanly or beyond our means.

The thirty-second chapter is about visiting a diviner, a person who claims to read signs of the future. You do not know what will come, but if you are a philosopher you already know what kind of thing it will be.
If the matter is not up to you, it cannot be good or evil, so do not bring desire or fear to the diviner. Whatever he says, you can use it well, and nobody can stop you.
Go to the gods as to wise advisers, and afterward remember whom you consulted. Socrates held that we should ask a diviner only when everything depends on the outcome and reason cannot answer.

So if you must share a friend's danger, or your country's, do not ask the diviner whether you should. If he says the omens are bad, he means death, injury or exile, but reason tells you to stand by your friend anyway.
So pay attention to the greater diviner, he says, Pythian Apollo, who spoke through the oracle at Delphi. He drove out of his temple a man who did not help a friend who was being killed.

The thirty-third chapter is the longest in the handbook, and it is full of advice about daily behaviour. It begins by telling you to fix a certain character for yourself and keep it when alone and with others.
Be silent for the most part, or say only what is necessary, and say it in few words. Now and then, when the occasion calls for it, you may speak, but not about ordinary things.
Do not talk about gladiators, horse races, athletes, food or drink, and above all do not talk about other people. Do not blame them, praise them or compare them.
If you can, steer the talk of others toward something fitting, but if you are among strangers, stay silent. Do not laugh much, or at many things, or without restraint, and avoid oaths if you can.

Know that if your companion is dirty, then anyone who spends time with him must become dirty too, even if he was clean. Avoid dinners given by outsiders and ignorant people, and if you must go, take care not to slip into their common habits.
Take the things of the body only as far as bare need, he says, such as food, drink, clothing, a house and servants. Cut off everything that is for show or luxury.
If someone tells you that a person is speaking ill of you, do not defend yourself. Just answer that he did not know your other faults, or he would not have mentioned only these.

If you go to the games, be eager for no one but yourself, wishing only that what happens should happen. Avoid shouting and laughing at anyone, and afterward do not talk much about it unless it helps you improve.
Do not go to people's readings of their own work too easily or rashly. But when you do go, keep your gravity and calm, and take care not to become disagreeable.

When you meet a person of high rank, ask what Socrates or Zeno would have done, and you will know how to behave. If the great man's door is shut, bear it and never say that the visit was not worth it.
In company, avoid talking often or at length about your own deeds and dangers. It is pleasant for you to tell of your risks, but it is not as pleasant for others to hear about your affairs.

Avoid trying to make people laugh as well, because it is a slippery path toward common behaviour and it lowers your neighbours' respect. It is also dangerous to slip into rude talk, and when it happens, show by silence or a frown that you dislike it.

The thirty-fourth chapter is about the pull of pleasure and the way to resist it. When a pleasure appears in your imagination, guard against being carried away by it, and let the thing wait while you give yourself time.

Then think of two moments: the time when you enjoy the pleasure, and the later time when you regret it and blame yourself. Set against these how glad you will be, and how you will praise yourself, if you hold back.

The thirty-fifth chapter says that when you do something you have judged right, you should never avoid being seen doing it. If the act is wrong, avoid it, but if it is right, why fear those who criticise you wrongly?

The thirty-sixth chapter uses a small example from logic to make a point about dinner. To choose the biggest portion may be of value for the body, but it is worthless for keeping the right character as a guest.
So when you dine with another person, remember not only what the food is worth to your body. Remember also to keep your respect for the host.
The thirty-seventh chapter warns about taking on a role that is beyond your strength. If you do, you will both disgrace yourself in it and neglect a role that you could have filled well.
The thirty-eighth chapter compares careful thinking to careful walking on a rough road. When you walk, you take care not to step on a nail or twist your foot.
In the same way, take care not to harm the ruling part of yourself, the part that judges and chooses. If we watch for this in every action, we will undertake each thing more safely.
The thirty-ninth chapter says that the body is the measure of what we need, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. If you stay within this measure, you will keep your balance.
If you go beyond it, you will be carried off as over a cliff. The shoe first becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered, because once the measure is passed there is no limit.
The fortieth chapter is a short remark about how people are valued. Epictetus says that people who put all their hopes in beauty should learn that they are honoured for modesty and self-respect.

The forty-first chapter says that it is a sign of a dull mind to spend a long time on things of the body. He means too much exercise, too much eating and drinking, and too much attention to bodily needs.
These things should be done in passing, as side matters, he says. Give your whole attention to the mind, because that is where your freedom is won.
The forty-second chapter explains why we can be gentle with people who wrong us. When someone does you harm or speaks ill of you, remember that he does it because he thinks it is right.
He cannot follow what seems right to you, only what seems right to himself. So if he judges wrongly, he is the one who is harmed, because he is the one who has been deceived.
Epictetus compares this to a true statement that someone takes to be false. The statement is not harmed by his mistake, but the person who has been deceived is.
Starting from this idea, you will be gentle with the person who insults you. On each occasion, say to yourself that it seemed so to him.
The forty-third chapter says that everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. If you pick up a jar by the wrong handle, you will not be able to lift it.

If your brother wrongs you, do not take it by the handle that he has wronged you, for it cannot be carried by that one. Take it by the other handle, that he is your brother and was brought up with you.
The forty-fourth chapter points out an argument that people often make without noticing. I am richer than you, therefore I am better, they say, or I speak better than you, therefore I am better.

The correct conclusion is more modest than the mistaken one, and it is easy to state. I am richer, so my property is greater, or I speak better, so my speech is better, but I am neither property nor speech.
The forty-fifth chapter is about the habit of judging other people too quickly. If someone bathes in a hurry, do not say that he bathes badly, but only that he bathes quickly.
If someone drinks a lot of wine, do not say that he drinks badly, but only that he drinks a lot. Before you know his reasons, how can you tell that he is acting badly?
The forty-sixth chapter says that you should never call yourself a philosopher. Do not talk much about principles among people who have not studied them, but do what follows from them.
For example, at a banquet do not say how one ought to eat, but eat as one ought. Epictetus wants our actions to do the speaking, and not our lectures about them.

Socrates avoided display so completely that when people wanted introductions to philosophers, he took them to the philosophers. He was perfectly content to be overlooked, and he never tried to be the centre of attention.
If talk about principles comes up among the untaught, stay mostly silent. There is great danger that you will spit out what you have not digested.
When someone tells you that you know nothing and you are not hurt, know that you have begun your work. A learner who needs no praise is on the right path.
Sheep do not show the shepherds how much they have eaten by bringing the grass. They digest it inside and produce wool and milk outside.
In the same way, do not show your principles to the untaught, but show the actions that come from digesting them. People will learn more from what you do than from what you say.
The forty-seventh chapter is about boasting of simple habits. Once you are used to living simply, do not take pride in it, and do not announce that you drink only water.
If you ever want to train yourself for endurance, do it for yourself and not for outsiders. When you are very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out and tell no one.

The forty-eighth chapter contrasts two kinds of person, starting with the ordinary one. He never expects benefit or harm from himself, only from outside things, while the philosopher expects all of it from himself.
Epictetus lists the signs of a person who is making progress. He blames no one, praises no one, complains of no one and accuses no one.

He does not talk about himself as if he were somebody important or knew a great deal. If someone praises him, he laughs privately at the praiser, and if someone blames him, he does not defend himself.
He goes about like an invalid, careful not to disturb anything that is healing before it has grown firm. A good habit that is still new needs the same gentle care as a mended bone.
He has removed desire from himself, and he turns his aversion only toward what is against nature among the things in his power. That means that he fears doing wrong far more than he fears any loss.
He uses only a moderate impulse toward everything he does. If he is thought to be foolish or ignorant, he does not care.
In a word, Epictetus says, such a person watches himself as if he were an enemy lying in wait. He is on guard not against others but against his own mistaken opinions.

The forty-ninth chapter deals with pride in learning, a trap for clever people. If someone is proud of explaining Chrysippus, say that he would have nothing to boast of if Chrysippus had written clearly.
What do I want, Epictetus asks, if not to learn nature and to follow it? If I cannot understand the writings of Chrysippus, I look for an interpreter, but so far nothing valuable has happened.

When I find the interpreter, what remains is to use the principles, and this alone is valuable. If I only admire the explaining, I have become a grammarian instead of a philosopher, except that I explain Chrysippus instead of Homer.
So when someone says, read me Chrysippus, I blush when I cannot show deeds that match his words. The fiftieth chapter then adds that whatever rules are set before you should be kept as laws.
Epictetus ends the fiftieth chapter with a short rule about what others say. Whatever anyone says about you, do not pay attention to it, because that is no longer your concern.
The fifty-first chapter is the most urgent of all. How long will you wait before you think yourself worthy of the best, he asks, and in nothing break the rules of reason?
You have received the teachings that you ought to agree with, and you have agreed with them. What teacher are you still waiting for, that you put off correcting yourself?
You are no longer a boy but a full-grown man, he says. If you keep putting things off, you will make no progress and will live and die an ordinary person.
So decide now that you are worthy to live as a full-grown man who is making progress. Let everything that seems best to you be a law that you do not break.
If something painful or pleasant or glorious or shameful is set before you, remember that now is the contest. Now are the Olympic Games, and it is no longer possible to put things off.
It is by a single day and a single action, Epictetus says, that progress is lost or saved. One moment of giving in can undo much, and one moment of holding firm can protect it.
Socrates became complete in just this way, by paying attention to nothing except reason in everything he met. He did not need to be perfect from the start, but only to keep choosing well each day.
You may not be Socrates yet, he says, but you ought to live as one who wishes to be Socrates. A good model does not need to be matched, but it needs to be followed.
The fifty-first chapter sums up the spirit of the whole handbook, which is to begin now. The best time to start practising what you have read is today, with the next small thing that happens to you.
The fifty-second chapter describes three topics that make up the study of philosophy. The first and most necessary is the use of principles, for example not to lie.
The second topic is demonstration, for example, why a person ought not to lie. This is where we give our reasons and arguments.

The third topic tests and examines these proofs, asking what a proof is, and what makes a statement true or false. It is the most technical part of the study, and the easiest to love for its own sake.
The third topic is needed because of the second, and the second is needed because of the first. So the first is the most necessary, and it is the place where we should rest.
But we do the opposite, Epictetus says, and spend our time and all our zeal on the third topic. So we lie, but we have the proof ready for why one should not.
Epictetus wants philosophy to be a way of acting. A person who argues well but lives badly has missed the point.

Epictetus was read, long after his death, by one of the most powerful people in the world. Marcus Aurelius, who ruled Rome from AD 161 to 180, wrote that his teacher Rusticus had lent him the lessons of Epictetus.
Around AD 530 a philosopher named Simplicius wrote a long commentary on the Enchiridion. It shows that people were still studying the handbook about four hundred years after Epictetus died.
In 1965 an American naval pilot, James Stockdale, was shot down over North Vietnam and held prisoner for years. He later said that the teaching of Epictetus helped him to face captivity.

Modern therapists such as Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck said that Stoic ideas about judgements influenced their methods. Today many people still quote the fifth chapter, about opinions and things, to explain how our thoughts shape our feelings.
The fifty-third and last chapter says that on every occasion we must keep three short sayings ready. They are short, but together they sum up the whole handbook.
The first is a prayer by Cleanthes, a Stoic who led the school after Zeno of Citium. Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you have placed me, and I will follow without hesitation.
If I am unwilling and become bad, the prayer goes on, I will follow all the same. So it is better to follow willingly, since there is no way to escape what happens anyway.
The second saying is from the poet Euripides, who lived in Athens in the fifth century BC. Whoever has nobly yielded to necessity, he says, is wise among us and knows divine things.
The third saying brings together two remarks of Socrates, as Plato records them. In one he tells his friend Crito that if this is what pleases the gods, then so let it be.
In the other, Socrates says that Anytus and Meletus can kill him, but they cannot harm him. They were the men who accused him at his trial in Athens in 399 BC.
The jury found Socrates guilty and sentenced him to death. He was calm to the end, and he spent his last day talking with his friends.
Epictetus returns to these ideas throughout his book, and a single question sums them all up. Each day, ask yourself whether the thing in front of you is up to you or not.
Then act on the answer, beginning with small things such as a spilled cup or a rude word. The handbook suggests that practice on trifles prepares you for the great tests.

The Enchiridion ends with three sayings: follow Destiny willingly, yield nobly to necessity, and remember that Socrates could not be truly harmed. Together they sum up the book, which promises that peace comes from meeting the world with a steady heart.
C1C2: Epictetus was born about AD 50 in Hierapolis, a town in what is now Turkey, and his Greek name, which means acquired, may have been no more than a label for a slave. Tradition says that he was born into slavery, yet his own life would become the best proof of what he taught, that no one can truly enslave a mind. Little else about his early years is certain, and the ancient writers who mention him do not always agree.

As a young man he was taken to Rome, where he served Epaphroditus, a freed slave who worked as a secretary to the emperor Nero. Tradition says that Epictetus became lame, though the stories differ: one blames a cruel master who twisted his leg, another a childhood illness. In his handbook he insists, with great calm, that lameness may hinder the leg but never the will.

Once he was freed, Epictetus attended the lectures of Musonius Rufus, a Roman Stoic who taught that philosophy was a craft to be practised daily and not merely a subject to be discussed. From Musonius he learned to speak plainly, to ask hard questions and to judge a teacher by the way he lived. Those habits, first learned in a crowded Roman lecture room, would stay with him through all his later years of teaching.

In about AD 93, though some historians place it earlier, the emperor Domitian ordered philosophers out of Rome, and Epictetus joined the exiles. He settled in Nicopolis, a young city in northwestern Greece that Augustus had founded to celebrate his victory at Actium. There he opened a school, and he taught there for many years to come.

His school was a plain room rather than a grand lecture hall, yet students travelled from across the Roman world to sit before a lame teacher who owned very little. He taught by questioning and argument, mixing jokes with blunt warnings, and he expected his listeners to change the way they lived. Visitors who wanted only clever talk about philosophy would often leave the room disappointed.

Epictetus wrote nothing himself, which was not unusual among ancient teachers who believed that philosophy lived in speech and in conduct. One of his students, Arrian, took careful notes and later published them as the Discourses, a long work in eight books, of which four have survived. Arrian said that he had set the words down as nearly as he could, in the very way they were spoken.

Arrian also picked out the most useful and memorable sayings and arranged them in a short handbook, the Enchiridion, for readers who wanted the heart of the teaching without the length. Its fifty-three brief chapters can be read in a single sitting, yet they are packed with advice that a person could carry into the market, the courtroom or the sickroom. For nearly two thousand years readers of every kind have kept coming back to it.

The Greek word enchiridion means something held in the hand, and in ancient usage it could refer both to a manual and to a small dagger. The double meaning suits the book well, for Epictetus meant his advice to be kept within reach and drawn whenever a difficult moment arrived. A handbook of this kind is not meant to sit on a shelf; it is meant to be used.

Epictetus belonged to the Stoic school, which was founded in Athens about 300 BC by Zeno of Citium and took its name from the painted colonnade, the Stoa, where Zeno liked to teach. Stoics held that the world is ordered by reason and that human beings find peace not by controlling events but by governing their own judgements. Later Stoics such as Musonius Rufus and Epictetus gave the old doctrine a practical, almost conversational, form.

Everything in the Enchiridion points toward a single promise, which is that a person can keep a steady and untroubled mind whatever fortune brings. The method is neither magical nor easy, and it begins with one sharp question that Epictetus asks us to put to everything we meet. The question is simply this: is it up to you, or is it not?

Epictetus opens his handbook with a single clean division of the world into what depends on us and what does not. Everything else in the book, he suggests, grows out of this one distinction, and every chapter in some way returns to it. A reader who truly understands this first page has already grasped the shape of the whole book.

The things that depend on us, he says, are our opinions, our impulses, our desires and our aversions, in short everything that is our own doing. These are the movements of the mind itself, and they are the only ground on which we are truly the masters. Whatever we want, whatever we fear and whatever we judge to be good or bad belongs here, and it is ours to shape.

The things that do not depend on us are our bodies, our property, our reputations and our public offices, in short everything that is not our own doing. Health can fail, wealth can vanish and fame can turn in a day, because each of them rests partly in the hands of other people and partly in the hands of fortune. Epictetus does not say that we should despise them, only that we should not mistake them for ours.

What is up to us, Epictetus explains, is free by nature, and nothing and no one can block it or hold it back. A tyrant may chain a man's leg and a thief may empty his house, but neither can compel him to hold a particular opinion or to make a particular choice. This is the kind of freedom that the whole handbook sets out to protect.

What is not up to us is weak, slavish and open to being taken away, because it is never fully in our hands and always belongs, in the end, to other people. We build our lives on it nonetheless, as though it were solid ground, and then we are shaken when the ground moves. Epictetus asks us to see this clearly and early, long before any loss has actually arrived.

If we mistake what is not ours for our own, he warns, we shall find ourselves blocked, grieved and troubled, and we shall blame gods and men alike for the harm. The anger we feel at the world is therefore a kind of mistake in bookkeeping, a claim made on goods that were never ours to claim. If we correct the mistake, much of the anger will have nowhere left to live in us.

But if we claim as ours only what really is ours, and treat the rest as belonging to others, then no one will be able to force us or hinder us, and we shall blame no one. We shall do nothing against our will, and we shall have no enemy anywhere in the world. No one will be able to do us harm, for no harm can touch what is truly ours.

Aiming at such great things, Epictetus warns, we must not go about it half-heartedly. Some things must be given up altogether, and others must be put off for the time being, if we are serious. If we try to chase office and wealth while also seeking this inner freedom, he adds, we may miss the office and wealth for trying to have both, but we will surely miss the freedom, which alone brings peace.

Epictetus then offers a practical method for hard moments, one that can be used on the spot. Whenever a harsh or frightening impression comes to us, we should say to it at once, You are only an impression, and not at all the thing you appear to be. The pause that this creates between the feeling and the judgement is, in effect, where our freedom begins.

Then, he says, we should examine the impression with the rule that we have, and first of all ask whether it concerns the things that are up to us or the things that are not. If it concerns what is not up to us, we must be ready to say, calmly, that it is nothing to us. It is a short sentence, but practising it for a lifetime is the whole task of the book.

The second chapter of the handbook explains why unhappiness follows so many of the plans that we make with such confidence. Desire promises us that we will get what we want, Epictetus says, and the person who fails to get what he desires is therefore unhappy. Every disappointment, in other words, is a promise broken, and we make the promises ourselves.

Aversion, the wish to escape what we dislike, works in exactly the same way, for it promises that we will avoid the thing and so leaves us wretched when the thing comes anyway. A man who dreads an illness, a quarrel or a bad harvest is quietly convinced that fortune owes him an escape. Epictetus suggests that fortune owes us nothing of the kind, and that we are wiser to expect nothing from it.

Epictetus names illness, death and poverty, the fears that haunt almost everyone, and he points out that none of them is up to us. If we fear what we cannot control, we shall never be at peace, because the fear will be waiting for us at every doorway. The cure, he says, is not courage alone but a clearer view of what is ours.

If aversion has been pointing at the wrong targets, where should it point instead, and what should we really be afraid of? Epictetus answers that it should be turned toward the things that are up to us and contrary to nature, which means our own wrong judgements and our own wrong acts. Fear, properly aimed, becomes a kind of guard, because those are the only dangers we can truly avoid.

For the present, he says, we should take desire away altogether from anything that is not up to us, because wishing for what we cannot command is the surest road to misery. This does not mean that we must turn cold or give up all hope, but that we must stop staking our peace on outcomes. The plan is to loosen our grip on the world, not to stop caring about the people and the work in it.

What is left is the plain impulse to choose and to refuse, and Epictetus tells us to use it lightly, gently and with reservation. To act with reservation means to keep in mind that the outcome may not be ours to command, so that a plan which fails is a surprise we can bear. The Stoics summed it up by saying, I shall do this, if nothing prevents it.

The third chapter turns to the things that charm us, serve us or are dear to us. Whenever we are fond of something, Epictetus advises, we should remind ourselves of what it really is, beginning with the smallest things such as a favourite clay jug. If it breaks, we shall then be no more disturbed than we expected to be, since we knew all along that a jug is the kind of thing that breaks.

He then moves, without any flinching, from the cups on our shelves to the people we love most in the world. When you kiss your child, Epictetus says, tell yourself that you are kissing a human being, and you will not be thrown into turmoil when the child dies. The point is not to love less but to love with open eyes, aware that every person we hold is mortal.

The fourth chapter begins with an ordinary scene that every reader of his day would have known, a visit to the public baths. Some people splash, others push, others shout and abuse one another, and some even steal, so a sensible bather prepares himself for what the place will really be like. A person who has pictured the crowd in advance will not be thrown off balance when someone elbows him in the water.

Having pictured the scene, Epictetus says, we should tell ourselves that we mean to bathe and also to keep our will in harmony with nature. If somebody splashes us or jostles us, we can then say that this was not the only thing we wanted, and that our own steadiness remains whole. The same preparation, he adds, should be made before every action we undertake, whether it is as small as a bath or as large as a journey.

The fifth chapter contains the sentence for which Epictetus is best remembered, that people are disturbed not by things themselves but by the opinions they hold about those things. A storm, an insult and a bad report from the doctor are all facts, but the pain that follows each one comes partly from the verdict we add to them. This is not a denial of hardship; it is an invitation to look for the place where our own hand has been at work.

Death, for instance, is nothing terrible in itself, Epictetus argues, or else it would have seemed terrible to Socrates. Socrates faced his own execution in Athens with cheerful composure, talking with his friends to the very end, and so he shows that dread is no part of death itself. What frightens us is the opinion that death is a terrible thing, and that opinion is something we are free to examine.

Whatever we call terror, then, lives in the opinion and not in the event, and that is the discovery on which the rest of the book is built. This is why Epictetus keeps sending us back to our judgements, since they are the one part of every troubling situation that we can actually reach. We cannot rewrite the weather, but we can examine the thoughts it provokes in us.

So when we are blocked, upset or grieved, he says, we should never blame anyone else but ourselves, by which he means our own opinions. It is a hard saying, because it is far more comfortable to find a culprit outside us. Yet a culprit outside us is also a jailer, since it hands the key to our peace to someone else.
