Epictetus sketches three stages of progress, and most of us can recognise ourselves in the first two. Untaught people blame others for their misfortunes, he says, beginners in philosophy blame themselves, and those who have been fully trained blame neither others nor themselves. The last stage is not about guilt at all; it is about seeing events for what they are.

The sixth chapter warns us against taking pride in anything that is not really our own. If a horse were to say proudly, I am beautiful, we might tolerate it as harmless, but when a man says, I have a beautiful horse, he is proud of the horse's good and not his own. The beauty belongs to the animal, and the man has merely been allowed a share in the sight of it.

The question that follows is obvious: what, then, is truly our own, and so a fair reason for pride? Epictetus answers that it is our use of impressions, meaning the way in which we receive, judge and act upon whatever happens to us. When we are proud of that, we are proud with good reason, for we are proud of a good that really belongs to us.

The seventh chapter compares life to a sea voyage, and the comparison is both gentle and exact. When the ship puts in at a harbour, a passenger may go ashore for fresh water and may pick up a small shell or a bulb along the way, but his mind must stay with the ship. The captain may call at any moment, and then all such trifles must be thrown away.

If you are given a wife and child instead of a shell and a bulb, Epictetus says, nothing prevents you from having them and enjoying them. But when the captain calls, you must run to the ship and leave everything behind without looking back. The picture is not cold, since it begins by welcoming the gifts, yet it never lets us forget that they are on loan.

If you are old, he adds, you should never go far from the ship, in case the captain calls and you are missing. The advice is practical as well as moving, for the older we grow the more carefully we should keep ourselves ready for the departure that is sure to come. Epictetus treats this readiness not as a gloomy thought but as a way of enjoying the shore with a quiet mind.

The eighth chapter contains a rule that sounds like surrender and works like a key. Do not ask that events should happen as you wish, Epictetus says, but wish them to happen as they do, and your life will go well. A person who follows this rule is not often disappointed by the world, because his wishes have been arranged to match it.

In the ninth chapter Epictetus considers two of the most familiar misfortunes that can befall a human body. Illness is a hindrance to the body, he says, and lameness to the leg, but neither is a hindrance to the will, unless the will itself consents. It is a sentence with a special weight in the mouth of a man whom tradition remembers as lame.

He asks us to repeat the thought on every occasion that comes our way, so that it becomes a habit rather than a slogan. If we do, we shall find that what has been hindered is always something else, and never ourselves. The leg may limp and the plan may fail, but the person who chooses and judges is still standing at the helm.

The tenth chapter offers a practical question that can be asked in the middle of almost any difficulty. On meeting any event, Epictetus says, turn to yourself and ask what faculty you have for dealing with it. This is a different habit from asking why it happened or who is to blame, and it turns every misfortune into a small exercise.

If you see someone handsome, Epictetus says, you will find that you have self-control, and if you meet hard work you will find endurance. If someone abuses you, you will find patience, and with practice the impressions that once carried us away will lose their hold on us. The capacity we need is almost always there; the trouble is that we forget to look for it.

The eleventh chapter changes the way we speak about loss, and Epictetus hopes that it will change the way we feel. Never say of anything that you have lost it, he writes, but say that you have given it back. The word is small, yet it turns a theft into a return and a victim into a borrower.

If your child dies, he says, the child has been given back, and so has your wife, if she dies. If your estate is taken, that too has been given back, and he asks you to treat it in the same spirit. These sentences sound severe, and perhaps they were meant to, because Epictetus knew how fiercely people cling to what they love.

But the man who took it is a wicked man, you may protest, and surely that changes everything. Epictetus replies with a question: what does it matter to you through whom the giver asked for his gift back? The question does not excuse the thief, but it does stop us from spending our peace on him.

While the gift is yours, he adds, take care of it as of something that is not your own, as travellers treat an inn. A traveller makes good use of the room and the bed and thanks the host, but he does not weep when the morning comes and he must leave. Seen this way, a whole life becomes a pleasant stay in a house that belongs to someone else.

Epictetus returns again and again to this picture of life as a loan, and it reshapes the way he asks us to hold everything we have. Our possessions, our work, our health and even the people closest to us are on loan, and gratitude is wiser than possessiveness. The lender will one day ask for his gift back, and the wise person has already made peace with that day.

The twelfth chapter is addressed to those who truly wish to make progress, and it asks them to give up a familiar kind of reasoning. Thoughts such as, if I neglect my affairs I shall have no income, and if I do not correct my slave he will turn out badly, are what keep us anxious from morning to night. Epictetus does not say that work and discipline do not matter; he says that peace of mind must not be made to depend on them.

It is better, he says, to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in plenty with a troubled mind. The sentence is extreme, and it makes us notice how much of our comfort we pay for with anxiety. Between the two there is a wide range of choices, of course, but the order of value is clear.

Begin with small things, Epictetus advises, because it is easier to learn calm over a trifle than over a catastrophe. If a little oil is spilled or a little wine is stolen, say to yourself that this is the price paid for peace of mind and for tranquillity. Each trifle borne well is practice for the larger losses that are certain to come.

Nothing is got for nothing, he reminds us, and that is as true of peace as of anything that is sold in the market. A calm mind has to be bought, and the coin we pay with is a willingness to lose small things without a fuss. Many people want the peace but refuse the price, and then they wonder why they are still restless.

When you call your servant, he adds, remember that he may not hear you, or may hear you and still not do what you ask. But he is not so powerful that your peace of mind should depend on his answer, and it would be foolish to hand him that much control. You may call calmly and wait calmly, whether he comes at once, comes late or does not come at all.

The thirteenth chapter makes a hard request of anyone who wants to improve: be content to be thought foolish and silly in matters that are outside you. Do not wish to be taken for a person who knows everything, he says, and if people begin to think that you are somebody important, learn to distrust yourself. It is a useful warning, because flattery is among the pleasantest ways of losing our way.

In the fourteenth chapter Epictetus calls it silly to wish that your children, your wife and your friends will live forever. Such a wish is for things that are not up to you, and so it amounts to wanting what belongs to someone else. Out of love we cannot help making that wish, yet the wish itself is a fragile place to keep our peace.

In the same spirit, he says, it is silly to wish that other people should never make a mistake, for that is to wish that a fault should not be a fault. People will go on erring as long as they are people, and no complaint of ours will change it. What we can change is whether we are surprised and wounded each time it happens.

But if you wish not to fail in your own desires, Epictetus says, you can do that, so you should practise on what you can do. This is the single piece of good news hidden in the long list of things we cannot control. The territory of our own desires and judgements is small, but it is entirely ours, and it is enough to live on.

He closes the chapter with a rule about freedom that sums up everything before it. Each person is master of whoever has power over the things that he wishes for or wishes to avoid, and so whoever wants to be free must neither wish for nor avoid anything that depends on others. If he does, he must necessarily be a slave, however many people may call him free.

The fifteenth chapter asks us to behave in life as we would at a banquet, and it is one of the most humane images in the book. When a dish is carried round to us, we put out a hand and take a polite share; we do not snatch, and we do not refuse in a way that offends the table. The wise guest enjoys whatever is offered, with good manners and with thanks, and never mistakes the dish for his own.

If the dish passes us by, we do not stop it or call it back, and if it has not yet reached us, we do not stretch our desire toward it but wait until it comes. The guest who grabs at the platter before his turn ruins the evening for everyone, and the guest who sulks when it goes past spoils his own. Patience, in this scene, is not a grim virtue but simply a form of good company at the table.

Epictetus says that we should treat children, a wife, an office and wealth in the same way, taking what is given with gratitude and waiting without grasping for what has not come. A person who lives like this will one day be a worthy partner in the banquet of the gods. The reward he names is not a prize but a companionship, and it is open to anyone who learns the manners.

From there the chapter goes a step further, and the step is a bold one. If we do not merely take what is set before us but are even able to despise it, he says, we shall be partners in the gods' rule as well as in their banquet. He names Diogenes and Heraclitus as men who earned that praise, and Diogenes was famous for living with almost nothing, while Heraclitus was an early thinker of Ephesus known for his riddling sayings.

The sixteenth chapter turns to a scene we all know, a friend weeping because his son has gone abroad or his property is lost. Take care, Epictetus says, not to be carried away by the impression that the man is in a real evil. Remind yourself instead that it is his judgement, and not the event itself, that distresses him, which is a way of keeping a clear head beside someone in pain.

Yet he does not ask us to stand aside, and he says plainly that we should not hesitate to comfort the man with words, and even to groan with him if the moment requires it. The one thing we must guard against is groaning inwardly too, for then we would have caught his mistaken judgement as if it were an illness. A friend who stays steady is more use than a friend who weeps beside us.

In the seventeenth chapter Epictetus asks us to remember that we are actors in a drama of the kind that the author wishes, short if he wants it short and long if he wants it long. We do not know the length of the play, the number of its acts or the day on which the curtain will fall. We know only that we have been given a part and that we are on stage.

If the author wants you to play a poor man, a lame man, a ruler or a private citizen, then play that part well, for that is your business. The choosing of the part belongs to somebody else, and no amount of complaining from the stage will rewrite the script. The actor who is given a small role and plays it with grace is worth more to the play than a star who sulks.

The eighteenth chapter deals with omens, which most people in his world took very seriously, and its example is a raven that croaks at an unlucky moment. Epictetus tells us not to be carried away by the impression but to distinguish and say that nothing of this is signified to us, but only to our body, our property, our reputation, our children or our wife. In other words, the omen at worst concerns outside things, and outside things are not where our wellbeing lies.

To me, he continues, every omen is favourable if I wish it to be, for whatever happens, it is in my power to benefit from it. A bird's cry, a failed plan or a bad piece of news may point toward a loss, but the way in which we meet the loss is still our own. That is the quiet confidence of a person who has taken the first chapter to heart.

The nineteenth chapter promises that we can be unbeatable, and the condition is simple. We must enter no contest in which victory does not depend on us, since the only contests we can be sure of winning are those fought on our own ground. A person who plays only on that ground is never defeated, because no one else can take the prize from him.

When we see someone honoured above others, or holding great power, or simply admired by everyone, we must take care not to be carried away by the impression and to pronounce him happy. We see the public part of his life, the procession and the praise, and we do not see what it may cost him in anxiety and effort. Epictetus asks us to hold back our verdict until we know where the good really lies.

If the essence of the good lies in what is up to us, he says, then there is no place for envy or jealousy, since nobody can take away what is truly ours. The envious man has already made a mistake about what is worth having, and his bitterness is the proof. When we have set our hearts on our own judgement and conduct, another person's success no longer subtracts anything from us.

We shall not wish, then, to be a praetor, a senator or a consul, which were the high offices of Rome, but to be free. The way to freedom, Epictetus insists, is contempt for the things that are not up to us, by which he means a refusal to let them rule us. A man may hold a high office and be a slave to it, while another holds nothing and answers to no one.

The twentieth chapter takes up a problem that nearly everyone knows from experience, the sting of an insult. Remember, Epictetus says, that it is not the person who reviles you or strikes you who insults you, but your opinion that these things are insulting. The other man provides the words or the blow, and we provide the injury, so the weapon is only half in his hands.

So when someone irritates you, he continues, it is your own opinion that irritates you, and the first rule is not to be carried away by the impression. If you can gain a little time and delay before you answer, you will find it far easier to master yourself. The pause may last no longer than a single deep breath, yet it is enough to separate the blow from the answer.

The twenty-first chapter asks us to keep before our eyes every day those things that appear terrible, above all death and exile. It is a strange exercise, and it is easy to mistake it for gloom, but Epictetus offers it as a way to loosen the grip of fear. What we have looked at calmly in advance can no longer take us entirely by surprise.

If we do this, he says, we shall never think anything abject and we shall never desire anything too much. A man who knows that he is mortal and that his comforts are borrowed has little reason to cringe before the powerful or to cling to small advantages. His wishes are kept in proportion because he has already seen the end of the road.

The twenty-second chapter gives a warning to anyone who feels the pull of philosophy. Be ready, says Epictetus, to be ridiculed and jeered at by many people, who will say that he has suddenly come back a philosopher and ask where he got that proud look. In every age the person who begins to take life seriously has been laughed at by those who find it more comfortable to go on as before.

Do not put on a proud look, Epictetus says, but hold to what seems best to you as a post assigned by a god. If you stand by the same principles, those who first ridiculed you will later admire you, but if you are overcome by them, you will be ridiculed twice. The advice is brief, and it carries a promise that steadiness is respected in the end.

The twenty-third chapter is a brief examination of motive, and it is one that most of us could usefully apply almost daily. If you ever turn toward outward show in order to please someone, Epictetus says, know that you have forfeited your plan of life. Be content to be a philosopher in everything, and if you also wish to seem one to anybody, appear so to yourself, for that will suffice.

The twenty-fourth chapter is one of the longest in the handbook, and it answers a worry that haunts almost everyone who tries to live quietly. Do not let such thoughts afflict you, Epictetus says, as I shall live without honour and be a nobody anywhere. The fear of being overlooked and forgotten is very old, and so, as we shall see, is his reply.

If lack of honour is an evil, he argues, then you cannot be in evil through another person any more than you can be in shame through him. Evils of that kind are brought on by our own choices, not by what others fail to give us. So the question to ask is not whether we are honoured but whether we have acted honourably.

Is it your business, he asks, to get a high post or to be invited to a dinner? Not at all, he answers, and so how can it be a dishonour to go without them? And how will you be a nobody anywhere, when you need to be somebody only in the one place that is in your power, where you can be of the greatest worth?

But your friends will be left without help, says an imagined objector, and surely a good friend would see to that. What do you mean by help, Epictetus replies, since they will not have money from you, and you cannot make them Roman citizens? Who told you that these things are in our power, and how can a person give what he does not own?

Then get them for us, says the objector, so that we may have them. If I can get them while keeping my honour, my loyalty and my dignity, Epictetus answers, show me the way and I will do it. But I will not lose my own good so that you may gain what is not good, and I ask you which you would rather have, money or a faithful and modest friend.

As for your country, the objector says, it will be left without your help. What help, Epictetus asks, since it will not get porticoes or baths from you, and in any case a smith does not supply shoes, nor a shoemaker weapons? It is enough, in his view, that each person does his own work well and does not pretend to do another's.

If you made one more citizen faithful and modest, Epictetus asks, would you do your country no good? Of course you would, the objector admits, and so you would not be useless to it. The place for you in the city is whatever place you can hold while staying faithful and modest, and nothing is gained if you lose both in the name of helping.

The twenty-fifth chapter asks us how to feel when another person is honoured before us, at a dinner, in a greeting or in being consulted. If these things are goods, we should be glad that he has them, and if they are evils, we should not be grieved that we do not. Epictetus then reminds us that those who do not do the same things cannot expect the same share.

A man who does not wait at another man's door cannot receive what the man who waits there receives, and one who does not praise cannot expect the reward of those who do. A lettuce costs perhaps an obol, a small coin, and if you do not pay it you have lost nothing, for you still have the coin. So when you are not invited to a dinner, you simply did not pay the host's price, which is praise and attendance, and what you have in its place is your own freedom from flattery.

The twenty-sixth chapter finds a lesson in a broken cup, and the lesson reaches much further than crockery. When a servant breaks another man's cup, Epictetus observes, we say at once that these things happen, and so when our own cup breaks we should be exactly as we were when the other broke. We learn the will of nature, he suggests, from the things on which we do not differ.

He asks us to carry the same attitude to greater things, which is a much harder test than a broken cup. When the child or wife of another person dies, there is no one who does not say that it is the human lot, but when our own is lost, we cry out, alas, wretched me. We should remember how we felt when we heard the same news about others, and let that memory teach us.

The twenty-seventh chapter is a single sentence, one of the strangest and most powerful in the whole handbook. Just as a target is not set up in order to be missed, Epictetus says, so nothing evil by nature exists in the world. Whatever we make of that claim, it invites us to look at events as parts of an ordered whole and not as strokes of malice aimed at us.

In the twenty-eighth chapter he asks us to imagine a scene that no one would accept. If someone handed over your body to any stranger who happened to meet you, you would be furious, and rightly so, because a body should not be shoved about by whoever passes. Yet most of us do something very like it every day, and we feel no shame about it.

We hand over our own minds, he says, to anyone who happens to insult us, allowing them to be disturbed and confounded. A passing stranger with a sharp tongue is allowed to do what we would never allow a stranger to do with our hands. The point is not to harden the heart but to guard the place from which we judge and choose.

The twenty-ninth chapter is one of the longest in the handbook, and its first lesson is to consider what comes before and after any action before we begin it. Otherwise we shall start with enthusiasm, and because we have not thought about the consequences, we shall give up in disgrace. Suppose, Epictetus says, that you wish to win at the Olympic Games, and he adds that he wishes it too, by the gods, for it is a fine thing.

But look first at what comes before and what follows, he says, and only then begin. The athlete must follow a strict order of life, keep to a diet, abstain from delicacies, and exercise under compulsion at the appointed hour in heat and in cold. He must hand himself over to his trainer as he would to a physician, and avoid cold water and wine unless they are prescribed.

Then, in the contest itself, he may be dug into the ditch, dislocate an arm, twist an ankle and swallow a great deal of dust. He may be whipped, and with all of this he may still be defeated. After weighing it all, Epictetus says, if the wish remains, go to the games, and if it does not, do not begin.

Otherwise, he warns, you will behave like children who play at wrestlers one day and gladiators the next, who blow trumpets and then act a tragedy. In the same way we try to be an athlete, then a gladiator, then an orator, then a philosopher, and with our whole soul nothing, like an ape imitating whatever it sees. Some people hear a speaker like Euphrates, who spoke so well, and immediately wish to be philosophers themselves.

Man, consider first what the matter is, Epictetus says, and then your own nature, and whether you can bear it. If you want to be a pentathlete or a wrestler, look at your arms, your thighs and your back, since different people are made for different things. Do you think that you can do this and still eat the same, drink the same and be as contented as before?

Epictetus then states plainly what the path will cost, and he does not flatter his reader. You must keep watch and labour, he says, leave your relatives, be despised by a slave and ridiculed by those who meet you, and come off worse in honour, in office, in the courts and in every petty matter. Consider whether you wish to pay that price for tranquillity, freedom and constancy, and if you do not, do not approach.

If you do not want to pay, he continues, then do not be like children, who are a philosopher now, a tax collector later, then a speaker and then an official of the emperor. These roles do not agree with one another, and you must be one person, good or bad, cultivating either your inner self or outside things. In other words, you must choose between the part of a philosopher and the part of an ordinary person.

The thirtieth chapter turns to duty, and its principle is that duties are in general measured by relationships. He is your father, and therefore you are told to take care of him, to give way to him in everything and to bear his reproaches and even his rough treatment. The sentence is hard, and it reflects the great authority of the Roman father in the world that Epictetus knew.

But he is a bad father, someone may reply, and the objection is a natural one. Epictetus answers by asking whether you were given a good father by nature, or only a father. The duty attaches to the relationship, he suggests, and does not rise or fall with the merit of the person who holds it.

The same reasoning applies to a difficult case from family life, the brother who wrongs you. Keep your own station toward him, Epictetus says, and consider not what he does but what you must do in order to keep your will in agreement with nature. For another person will not harm you unless you choose, and you will be harmed only when you think that you are harmed.

In this way, he concludes, you will find your duties as a neighbour, as a citizen or as a general, if you accustom yourself to look at the relationship each time. The method is as simple as it is useful, and it begins with asking, in any dealing with another person, who this person is to me. Duty becomes a matter of seeing clearly instead of a matter of feeling like it.

The thirty-first chapter turns to the gods, and it says that the chief part of piety is to hold right opinions about them, as beings who exist and who govern all things well and justly. We must set ourselves to obey them, yield to all that happens and follow willingly, as to the work of the wisest intelligence. In this way, Epictetus says, we shall never blame the gods or accuse them of neglecting us.

That cannot be done, he adds, unless we withdraw from things that are not up to us and place good and evil only in what is. If we count outside things as good or evil, we shall blame and hate whoever seems to stand in the way, since every creature is made to flee what harms it. This is why the farmer, the sailor and the merchant, and those who lose their wives and children, revile the gods, for where a person's interest lies, there his piety lies too.

To show how a mistaken opinion can wreck a relationship, Epictetus offers a famous example from Greek legend. Polynices and Eteocles, who fought over the throne of Thebes, became enemies because each of them thought that the throne was a good. A father is likewise reviled by his son when he does not give him what the son thinks is good, and so a false opinion about what is valuable turns brothers into rivals.

Piety also has a practical side, he adds, and it follows the habits of the place where we live. We should make our offerings, sacrifices and first fruits according to the custom of our country, purely, and not carelessly or meanly or beyond our means. The advice is characteristically moderate, since it asks neither for stinginess nor for show, only for sincerity and good sense.

The thirty-second chapter deals with a practice that most people in the ancient world took for granted, going to a diviner, a person who claimed to read signs of the future. When you go, Epictetus says, remember that you do not know what will come, since that is why you have come, but you do know what kind of thing it will be if you are a philosopher. If it is among the things that are not up to us, it can be neither good nor evil.

So you should not bring desire or aversion to the diviner, and you should not tremble before him, since you have already understood that every outcome is indifferent and nothing to you. Whatever it may be, you can use it well, and no one will be able to prevent that. Go confidently to the gods as to counsellors, and afterwards, when something is advised, remember whom you took as counsellors and whom you would be disregarding if you ignored them.

Epictetus adds that Socrates thought we should go to divination in cases where the whole inquiry concerned the outcome and no means were given by reason or any craft for finding it out. These are the rare cases, and for the rest we are expected to use our own judgement. The oracle, in this view, is a last resort and not a way of escaping the work of thinking.

So when you must share the danger of a friend or of your country, you should not ask the diviner whether you ought to do so. If the diviner says that the omens are bad, it is plain that death, the loss of a limb or exile is foretold, yet reason demands that even so you stand by your friend. Some questions have already been answered, in advance, by the kind of people we have chosen to be.

Heed instead, he says, the greater diviner, Pythian Apollo, who spoke through the oracle at Delphi and who threw out of his temple the man who did not help his friend while the friend was being killed. The handbook gives no further details of the story, but its meaning is plain enough. There is no oracle, however holy, that can excuse a person from loyalty to a friend.

The thirty-third chapter is the longest in the handbook, and it reads like a set of rules for ordinary life, from conversation to dinner parties to the way we laugh. It begins by telling us to establish a certain character and pattern for ourselves, which we shall keep both when we are alone and when we are with other people. A person who behaves in one way in private and another in public has two selves, and neither of them is at peace.

Be silent for the most part, Epictetus advises, or say only what is necessary and in a few words. We may speak, though rarely, when the occasion calls for it, but not about the common topics of the day. The advice is easy to give and difficult to follow, because nearly every conversation invites us to say more than we mean.

He lists the topics to avoid: gladiators, horse races, athletes, food and drink, which were the sports and pleasures of his day, and above all people, whether in blame, in praise or in comparison. If you can, he says, bring the talk of others by your own words to something fitting, but if you find yourself among strangers, be silent. It is a modest rule, but anyone who kept it would find that most dinner tables sounded very different.

Do not laugh much, he says, nor at many things, nor without restraint, and take care that your amusement does not run away with you. Refuse oaths altogether if you can, and if you cannot, refuse them as far as circumstances allow. These small disciplines belong together, for each of them keeps the mind from being swept along by the mood of the crowd.

Know that if your companion is dirty, then whoever spends time with him must become dirty too, even if he himself was clean. For this reason Epictetus advises us to avoid banquets given by outsiders and by ignorant people, and if the occasion arises, to be strictly careful not to slip into the common manner. The company we keep is a kind of weather, and over time it leaves its mark on us.

Take the things that concern the body only as far as bare need requires, Epictetus advises, such as food, drink, clothing, house and servants, and cut away everything that is for show or luxury. It is the habit of a person who has decided where his real treasure lies and does not wish to spend it on the wrong things. A plain life is not a punishment in his eyes but a way of travelling light.

If someone tells you that a certain person has been speaking ill of you, do not defend yourself, but answer that he did not know your other faults, or else he would not have mentioned only these. The reply is a witty one, and it takes the sting out of the gossip by agreeing, in good humour, that we are far from perfect. A person who is not afraid of his own faults is very hard to wound with anyone else's words.

When you go to the public games or the theatre, show yourself eager for no one but yourself, which means wishing only that what happens should happen and that the winner should be the one who truly wins. In this way, Epictetus says, you will not be hindered, because you are no longer standing on the outcome. Refrain entirely from shouting, from laughing at anyone and from any great excitement of feeling, however loud the crowd around you.

And after you have left, he adds, do not talk much about what took place, except in so far as it contributes to your improvement, for otherwise it would show that you were struck with admiration for the spectacle. Do not go to people's readings rashly or easily, either, but when you do go, keep your gravity and your calm, and avoid being disagreeable. The advice recalls how easily an entertainment can take over a mind that has no business of its own.

When you are going to meet someone of reputed superior rank, put before yourself what Socrates or Zeno would have done, and you will not lack the means to deal with the occasion properly. When you call on a powerful man, remind yourself that he may not be at home, that you may be shut out and that the door may be slammed in your face. If it is still fitting to go, go, and bear what happens, and never say that it was not worth it, for that is the remark of someone who is affected by outside things.

In company, Epictetus says, we should avoid frequent and excessive talk about our own deeds and dangers. It may be pleasant for you to recall your adventures, but it is not equally pleasant for others to hear about your affairs. Nearly everyone has met the guest who turns every conversation toward himself, and nobody has ever wished to sit next to him twice.

Avoid also provoking laughter, he says, for it is a slippery way toward commonness and at the same time enough to diminish the respect of your neighbours. It is dangerous too to slip into obscene talk, and when that happens, if there is an opportunity, rebuke the one who has begun it. If there is not, show by silence, by blushing or by frowning that you are displeased.

The thirty-fourth chapter turns to the pull of pleasure, which is among the oldest of our weaknesses. When a pleasure is presented to your imagination, he says, take care that it does not carry you away, as with any other impression, but let the thing wait for you and give yourself a delay. The pause is a small gap in which our judgement has room to work.

Then call to mind two times, Epictetus says: the time when you will enjoy the pleasure, and the later time when you will repent and reproach yourself. Set against these the thought of how you will rejoice and praise yourself if you abstain. If it seems right to go ahead, take care that its charm and attraction do not overcome you, and set against them how much better it is to be conscious of having conquered them.

The thirty-fifth chapter is about courage of a quiet and everyday kind, the courage to be seen doing right. When you do something that you have judged ought to be done, never shrink from being seen doing it, even if most people think otherwise about it. If the act is not right, avoid the act itself, but if it is right, why should you fear those who find fault with you wrongly?

The thirty-sixth chapter begins with an example from logic, in which the statements it is day and it is night are of great value in one kind of proposition and of none in another. In the same way, Epictetus says, choosing the largest portion at a feast has value for the body but is worth nothing for keeping up the character of a guest. A dinner is, among other things, a quiet test of good manners and of self-command.

So when you dine with another person, remember to look not only at the value for your body of the things set before you, but also at the respect that you owe the host. A guest who counts every dish as a prize has forgotten that he is in someone's house and among friends. The meal feeds the body, but the manner of eating feeds the character, and the host will remember the second.

The thirty-seventh chapter warns against taking on a role that is beyond your strength. If you do, Epictetus says, you will both disgrace yourself in it and neglect the one that you might have filled well. It is a warning against ambition without self-knowledge, and it is one of the gentlest in the handbook.

The thirty-eighth chapter compares moral care to the care we take when we walk. As you are careful not to step on a nail or to twist your ankle, so you should take care not to harm the ruling part of yourself, which is the part that judges and chooses. A nail in the foot is quickly noticed, but an injury to our judgement can go unfelt for years.

If we watch over that part in every action, he says, we shall undertake each action more safely. The habit is to stop before acting and to ask whether what we are about to do will leave our judgement sound or damaged. Most of the harm that people do themselves begins in some small decision that they did not pause over.

The thirty-ninth chapter offers a precise and memorable image of how much is enough for a person to own. The measure of possession for each person is the body, Epictetus says, just as the foot is the measure of the shoe, and if we stand on this measure we shall keep within limits. A shoe that is larger than the foot is not a better shoe but only a more awkward one.

If we go beyond that measure, he warns, we shall be carried over a cliff, and the same happens with the shoe. First it must be gilded, then it must be purple, then it must be embroidered, for once the measure is passed there is no limit. The desire for more is a road that has no natural end, and the only way to be done with it is to stop where the body stops.

The fortieth chapter is a short remark that sounds awkward to modern ears, and it concerns people who are valued only for their looks. Epictetus observes that such people begin to adorn themselves and to place all their hopes in it, and that we should make them understand that they are honoured only for modest behaviour and self-respect. Whatever we think of its examples, the point is that character, not appearance, earns lasting respect.

The forty-first chapter says that it is a sign of a dull mind to spend much time on things of the body, such as much exercise, much eating and drinking, and the rest of the body's business. He does not tell us to neglect health, only that these matters should not fill our days. A mind that has been allowed to grow lazy will make a poor guide, however strong the body it lives in.

These things should be done by the way, he says, as side matters, and all of our attention should be turned to the mind. A person who gave to the mind even a little of the care that he gives to his comforts would soon see the difference in his life. The call is for balance rather than neglect, and it is made without apology.

The forty-second chapter explains why we can afford to be gentle with people who wrong us. When someone does you harm or speaks ill of you, Epictetus says, remember that he does or says it because he thinks it right. It is not possible for him to follow what seems right to you, but only what seems right to himself.

So if a man judges wrongly, he is the one who is harmed, since he is the one who has been deceived. Epictetus compares this to someone who takes a true statement to be false, for in that case the statement is not harmed, but the person who has been deceived is. Our anger is aimed at the wrong target, because the one who has the real injury is the one who made the mistake.

Starting from this idea, you will be gentle toward the person who reviles you, saying on each occasion, it seemed so to him. The sentence is short enough to remember in the middle of a quarrel, and it changes the question from how dare he to what does he believe. Understanding a person's mistake is not the same as agreeing with it, but it makes revenge look a good deal less necessary.

This way of looking at things has a practical benefit, which is that it spares us a great deal of trouble. Anger that has been answered with anger tends to double itself, while anger that has been answered with patience often has nowhere to go. The method does not guarantee peace, but it keeps our own side of the quarrel quiet.

The forty-third chapter gives one of the handbook's best-loved images, that everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. A jar that is lifted by its handle comes up easily, but the same jar gripped by its smooth side slips and breaks. Almost every situation in life offers us a choice of this kind, and we often pick up the wrong handle without noticing.

If your brother wrongs you, Epictetus says, do not take it by the handle that he is wronging you, for that is the handle by which it cannot be borne. Take it rather by the other, that he is your brother and was brought up with you, and then it can be carried. The injury is the same in both cases, but what we pick up and what we leave on the ground is our choice.

The forty-fourth chapter picks out a very common mistake in reasoning, in which we turn a fact about what a person has into a conclusion about what he is. I am richer than you, therefore I am better, someone says, or, I am a finer speaker than you, therefore I am better. Neither argument holds, because the first fact tells us about property and the second about speech, and neither of them tells us about character.

The sound conclusions are much more modest than that, Epictetus says, and they are easy to state in their proper form. I am richer than you, therefore my property is greater than yours, and I am a finer speaker, therefore my speech is better than yours, but you are neither property nor speech. This leaves room for admiring a gift without bowing to the person who has it, and for having a gift without growing proud of it.

The forty-fifth chapter is a lesson in not judging too fast, and it begins with a trip to the baths again. If someone bathes quickly, do not say that he bathes badly, but only that he bathes quickly, because the first is a verdict and the second is only what you saw. A verdict needs a reason behind it, and the reason lives inside the other person's head, where we cannot see.

If someone drinks a great deal of wine, do not say that he drinks badly but only that he drinks a great deal. Before you have understood his opinion, how can you know that he is acting badly? By describing what we saw before we pass a verdict, he says, we avoid agreeing too quickly to impressions that we have not examined.

The forty-sixth chapter begins with a rule of modesty that is easy to state and hard to keep. Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, and do not talk much among the untaught about principles, but do what follows from them. A teacher who lectures all day and lives badly has taught nothing, and a quiet neighbour who lives well has taught a great deal.

At a banquet, for example, do not say how one ought to eat, but eat as one ought. The philosopher's argument is made with a knife and a cup and with good manners toward the people who sit around him. It is far easier to explain what is right than to do it quietly, without an audience.

Remember that Socrates avoided display so completely that when people came to him wanting to be introduced to philosophers, he took them to the philosophers himself. He was so patient of being overlooked, Epictetus says, that he seems to have wanted no credit at all. Socrates is the model in nearly every chapter of the handbook, and here he is the model of modesty.

If talk about principles comes up among the untaught, Epictetus says, you should be silent for the most part, since there is great danger that you will spit out what you have not digested. The image is a vivid one, and it is aimed at the eager beginner who has just read a good book and wants to tell everyone about it. Half-understood wisdom, repeated too soon to the wrong audience, does more harm than honest silence would have done.

And when someone tells you that you know nothing, and you are not hurt, know that you have begun the work. It is a surprising test, for it measures progress not by what we can say but by what no longer wounds us. The learner who still needs to be admired has not yet found the ground on which to stand.

Sheep, Epictetus says, do not show the shepherds how much they have eaten by bringing the grass to them, but digest their food inside and produce wool and milk outside. The point of the comparison is that a good principle shows itself in results, and the results of eating are far more useful than the grass itself. A person who has really taken in what he has read will be recognised by what he does.

So do not display principles to the untaught, he concludes, but show the actions that come from digesting them. The forty-seventh chapter then adds a warning about a related temptation, which is to boast of our hardness. When you have become used to a simple way of living in matters of the body, do not take pride in it, and do not say on every occasion that you drink only water.

If you ever wish to train for endurance, Epictetus says, do it for yourself and not for outsiders. Do not go about embracing statues, as Diogenes was said to do in winter, but practise in private where no one is watching. An exercise of self-control that depends on being admired by others has already failed in its purpose.

When you are very thirsty, he adds, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out and tell no one. The exercise is tiny, a mouthful of water that is never swallowed, and it is done in secret so that the self-denial stays real. Training of this kind is a conversation with ourselves, and it needs no witnesses.

The forty-eighth chapter, one of the richest in the handbook, contrasts two kinds of person in a few clear sentences. The ordinary person, Epictetus says, never expects benefit or harm to come from himself but only from outside things, while the philosopher expects all benefit and all harm to come from himself. Everything else in this long and important chapter follows from that difference in where we look.

Epictetus lists the signs of a person who is making progress, and the list reads like a portrait of someone we should like to meet. He blames no one, praises no one, complains of no one and accuses no one, and he says nothing of himself as if he were somebody or knew something. When he is hindered or prevented, he does not look for someone to blame but turns first to his own judgement.

If someone praises him, he laughs privately at the person who praises him, and if someone censures him, he does not defend himself. It is not that he enjoys being disliked, but that he has stopped depending on the verdicts of others for his sense of who he is. Praise and blame are weather, and he dresses for it without arguing with the clouds.

He goes about like an invalid, Epictetus says, careful not to disturb anything that is getting well before it has grown firm. A good habit that is still young needs the same gentle care as a mended bone, and the same patience while it hardens. The comparison reminds us that progress in character is slow and fragile, and that it may be undone by one careless week.

He has taken away desire from himself entirely, and he has transferred aversion only to those things among the ones in our power that are contrary to nature. In other words, he has stopped fearing illness, poverty and bad luck, and he fears instead acting badly. The change is not one of mood but of aim, as when an archer moves from one target to a better one.

He uses moderate impulse toward everything, Epictetus continues, and if he is thought foolish or ignorant, he does not care. A person who has stopped needing a reputation for cleverness has laid down one of the heaviest burdens that people carry. He has discovered that being thought wise and being wise are two quite different things.

In a word, Epictetus concludes, such a person watches himself as an enemy lying in wait, ready to catch each mistaken opinion as it appears. The picture is a startling one, but it is not unkind, because the enemy he is guarding against is not any other person but the careless, vain or fearful part of himself. A watchman of that sort does not hate the city he guards, and Epictetus has no hatred for the self that he asks us to watch.

The forty-ninth chapter deals with pride in learning, a vice that philosophers have always found it easy to fall into. When someone prides himself on being able to understand and interpret the books of Chrysippus, Epictetus says, tell yourself that if Chrysippus had not written obscurely, this man would have nothing to be proud of. Chrysippus was a famous Stoic of the third century BC who is said to have written hundreds of books.

What do I want, Epictetus asks, if not to learn nature and to follow it? So I ask who can explain nature, and I hear that it is Chrysippus, but I cannot understand his writings and must look for an interpreter. So far nothing valuable has happened, he says, for all of this is only the road to the real thing.

When I find the interpreter, what remains is to use the precepts, and this alone is valuable. But if I merely admire the exposition, I have become a grammarian instead of a philosopher, except that I interpret Chrysippus instead of Homer. So when someone says, read me Chrysippus, I blush when I cannot show deeds that match and echo his words.

The fiftieth chapter is brief and firm, and it is addressed to anyone who has chosen rules for their own life. Whatever has been set before you as a rule, abide by it as by a law, as though it would be wrong to break it. A person who keeps a few good rules faithfully will do better than one who admires a great many without following any.

The fiftieth chapter ends with a sentence about the opinions of other people that are certain to come. Whatever anyone says about you, Epictetus tells us, pay no attention to it, for that is no longer your concern. Once you have chosen your rules, the chatter of other people becomes a kind of weather that you may notice but are not obliged to obey.

The fifty-first chapter is the most urgent in the handbook, and it reads like a hand laid on the reader's shoulder. How long will you wait, Epictetus asks, before you think yourself worthy of the best, and in nothing transgress the distinctions of reason? The questions come one after another, and they have the force of a coach who has run out of patience.

You have received the precepts that you ought to agree with, he says, and you have agreed with them. What teacher, then, are you still waiting for, that you put off correcting yourself until he arrives? The question is an uncomfortable one, since most of us go on collecting teachers and books in the hope that a better one will make the work easier.

You are no longer a boy, he says, but a full-grown man, and the time for excuses has already passed. If you are careless and slothful, and make delay after delay, and fix one day after another as the day when you will attend to yourself, you will not notice that you are making no progress. You will live and die an ordinary person, and the warning is stern, but it is the sternness of a friend who would rather see you wake up now.

So decide now, Epictetus says, that you are worthy to live as a full-grown man who is making progress, and let everything that seems best be a law to you. The sentence is both generous and demanding, for it treats us as capable of greatness and then asks us to prove it. Notice that he does not say to become perfect, only to treat the best that you know as binding.

If anything painful or pleasant or glorious or inglorious is set before you, remember that now is the contest, now are the Olympic Games, and it is no longer possible to put things off. The image returns to the athlete of the twenty-ninth chapter, and it tells us that the games are not held in some other season. They are held every day, in the small choices of temper, appetite and honesty that nobody applauds.

By a single day and a single action, Epictetus says, progress is lost or saved. The claim is a warning, but it is also a comfort, because it means that no failure is final and that a single good decision can still turn the day. Our whole history of mistakes weighs less than the present moment, in which the next choice is still unmade.

Socrates became perfect in this way, Epictetus says, by paying attention to nothing except reason in everything he encountered. He was a soldier, a husband and a citizen of Athens who met ordinary troubles, and he met them by asking the same question every time. The question was what reason required, and it led him, in the end, to a prison cell and a cup of poison, which he took without complaint.

And you, even if you are not yet a Socrates, ought to live as one who wishes to be Socrates. This is a gentle standard, because it does not demand that we have arrived but only that we are facing in the right direction. A traveller who walks toward the harbour every day will get there, however slowly.

Taken together, the fifty-first chapter rings like a bell at the end of a lesson. It does not teach a new idea but presses the old ones into the present moment, with the message that the time to begin is today and not some better season. Whatever has been understood in the earlier pages is now to be tried on the next small thing that goes wrong.

The fifty-second chapter gives philosophy an order of work, and the order turns out to be a pointed criticism of how many people study it. The first and most necessary topic, Epictetus says, is the use of principles, and his example is the principle that one must not lie. Everything else in philosophy, he suggests, exists to serve this plain, practical business of actually behaving well.

The second topic is demonstration, which means giving the reasons, for example why one ought not to lie. Here the philosopher explains the principle and shows that it follows from what is true about human beings and the world. Reasons make a principle stronger, but a reason is useful only when there is a principle already being practised.

The third topic is the one that confirms and analyses the first two, asking such questions as why this is a demonstration, what a demonstration is, and what counts as a consequence, a contradiction, a truth or a falsehood. The Stoics were famous for their logic, and this part of philosophy could become as fine and difficult as any craft. Epictetus does not despise it, but he knows how easily a student can fall in love with the machinery.

The third topic is necessary because of the second, he says, and the second because of the first, so that the most necessary of all, and the one where we should rest, is the first. The order is like that of a building, in which the foundations carry the walls and the walls carry the roof, and a roof held up by nothing is only a heap of tiles. A student who spends his years in the upper rooms of logic has built nothing to stand on.

But we do exactly the opposite, Epictetus says, for we spend our time on the third topic and put all our zeal into it, while neglecting the first altogether. The result is a person who lies, and who has the demonstration ready why one ought not to lie. The joke is a bitter one, and it is aimed at every clever person who has ever known better than he behaved.

The point of the whole chapter is that philosophy is a way of acting before it is a way of talking. A person who argues brilliantly and lives badly has missed the purpose, while a person who lives well without any theory has already learned the best part. Before the final chapter, it is worth pausing to ask what became of this small book after Arrian first wrote it down.

Epictetus was read, long after his death, by some of the most powerful people in the world. Marcus Aurelius, who ruled Rome from AD 161 to 180 and kept a private notebook of Stoic reflections, recorded that his teacher Rusticus had lent him the lessons of Epictetus from his own library. The emperor who ruled a vast empire had thus been taught by a man who, tradition says, had once been a slave himself.

Around AD 530, nearly four hundred years after Epictetus died, a philosopher named Simplicius wrote a long commentary on the Enchiridion. The existence of such a work shows that the little handbook was still studied and explained in the schools of late antiquity. Books survive when people keep finding reasons to copy them, and this one gave them plenty.

In 1965 an American naval pilot named James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam and held prisoner for years. He later said that the teaching of Epictetus, which he had met earlier as a student, helped him to face captivity, above all the idea of separating what he could control from what he could not. The story shows the handbook doing what a handbook is meant to do, which is to go with a person into the hardest rooms of life.

In the twentieth century, therapists such as Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck said that Stoic ideas about judgements had influenced the methods that they developed. Their treatments rest on a familiar observation, that our distress is shaped by the way we interpret events and that those interpretations can be examined and changed. It is nearly the same observation that Epictetus placed at the head of his fifth chapter, and many people still quote it to explain how thoughts shape feelings.

The fifty-third and last chapter tells us that on every occasion we should have three sayings ready at hand, as a traveller keeps a few coins in a pocket. The sayings are short, and each belongs to a different voice, a Stoic teacher, a poet and a philosopher who faced death. Together they gather up the whole handbook, as the last page of a letter gathers up what the writer most wished to say.

The first is the prayer of Cleanthes, the Stoic who led the school after Zeno of Citium and who is remembered for a hymn to Zeus. Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you have assigned me, he prays, and I will follow without hesitation. Epictetus quotes the lines because they turn acceptance into a willing choice rather than a defeat.

If I am unwilling, the prayer goes on, and become bad, I shall follow nonetheless. The second half is bracing, because it admits that the world will not wait for our agreement, and so the only freedom left to us is the freedom to follow willingly or unwillingly. A person who follows with a grumbling heart gets the same road as one who follows gladly, but travels it in far worse company.

The second saying comes from the Athenian poet Euripides, who died in 406 BC and wrote some of the best-known tragedies of the ancient stage. Whoever has nobly yielded to necessity, he says, is wise among us and knows divine things. The word nobly matters here, for it is the manner of yielding, with dignity and without resentment, that makes it wise.

The third saying brings together two remarks of Socrates, as Plato records them, and both were spoken when his life was in danger. In the first, he tells his friend Crito, in the prison where he was waiting to die, that if this is what pleases the gods, then so let it be. The remark is quiet and almost cheerful, and it shows how far a person may travel toward acceptance without ever losing his courage.

In the second remark, Socrates says that Anytus and Meletus can kill him but cannot harm him. They were among the men who accused him before an Athenian jury in 399 BC, charging him with failing to honour the gods of the city and with corrupting the young. The jury found him guilty and sentenced him to death, and the sentence was carried out after a delay of some weeks.

Socrates met his sentence with a calm that moved his friends, and according to Plato he spent his last day talking with them about the soul and whether it survives death. At the end he drank the poison that the state provided, and he spoke kindly to the man who gave it to him. Epictetus holds him up throughout the handbook as the model of a mind that no accuser can touch.

Looking back over the whole handbook, we can see that its lessons rest on a single question, which can be asked at any moment of any day: is this up to me, or is it not? The question costs nothing to ask, but a lifetime of asking it is what turns a clever idea into a quiet habit of mind. Nearly every chapter of the book is really an example of what to do once we have found the answer.

Epictetus advises us to practise on small things first, as athletes train before they compete. A spilled cup, a rude word, a delayed meal and a lost coin are all small rehearsals for the great tests of illness, loss and death. In each of them we can ask whether we are keeping the right opinion, and so build, little by little, the habits that will hold when the stakes are high.

The Enchiridion closes with three short sayings that, Epictetus says, we should keep ready on every occasion. The first, a prayer by the Stoic Cleanthes, asks Zeus and Destiny to lead us wherever they please and promises to follow without hesitation, while the second, from the poet Euripides, calls wise anyone who has nobly yielded to necessity. The third is the calm word of Socrates, that his accusers could kill him but never truly harm him, and together they sum up the book: peace comes from meeting the world with a steady heart.
